title: Appraisers and Assessors of Real Estate
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For appraisers and assessors of real estate broadly, the rising demand for smaller "shallow-bay" warehouse formats alters the criteria used to collect and analyze relevant data to identify real estate market trends [1]. This shift requires a modification of how workers compute final estimation of property values by introducing new comparative benchmarks for last-mile distribution assets versus traditional big-box industrial properties [1], [2]. The mechanism is a change in the "highest and best use" analysis, where smaller, service-oriented footprints now command different market premiums than larger warehouses [1]. Because professional standards require physical verification of asset condition, the task of inspecting properties to determine appraisal value is unlikely to change [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, industrial real estate valuation will shift toward more granular, format-specific comparative market analyses to account for the rise of last-mile distribution assets.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

If current trajectories in industrial fragmentation hold, for appraisers and assessors of real estate broadly, valuation models may transition from simple square-footage metrics to higher-resolution utility analysis. This shift could affect the task of analyzing trends in sales prices and rents, as the value of shallow-bay properties becomes more dependent on hyper-local logistics networks than regional industrial trends [1], [2]. However, the requirement to search public records for transactions remains a structural necessity to ensure the accuracy of the data used in these updated models [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may see a divergence in valuation methodologies between bulk industrial assets and specialized, high-utility urban logistics nodes.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For appraisers and assessors of real estate broadly, the persistence of the shallow-bay trend may lead to a fundamental decoupling of industrial property value from traditional zoning categories. One rival outcome involves a shift toward dynamic valuation based on real-time throughput data, while another suggests a consolidation back to larger hubs if distribution technology evolves beyond last-mile vehicle dependencies. It remains unknown how evolving urban zoning laws will reconcile industrial shallow-bay demand with residential proximity. The task of testifying in court as to the value of a piece of real estate is likely to resist change because the legal system requires a named professional to assume liability for the valuation [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, industrial appraisal may integrate real-time operational data into the computation of property values for logistics assets.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the demand for shallow-bay properties may collapse in favor of centralized automated hubs, returning industrial appraisal to a big-box valuation model.*

title: Budget Analysts
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For budget analysts in government settings, the impact of new fiscal frameworks varies by organizational objective. In municipal governments implementing livable wage policies, work may shift toward higher-frequency modeling of payroll impacts because increasing wages may force trade-offs between taxes and spending [1]. These analysts could apply more rigorous cost-benefit analyses to compare operating programs and explore alternative financing methods [3] as payroll becomes a more volatile expenditure. Meanwhile, for analysts in government settings adopting digital and data benefit frameworks, there is a shift toward quantifying the financial and non-financial benefits of digital programs to justify funding and resource allocation [2]. This alters how analysts compile and analyze accounting records to determine the financial resources required to implement a program [3]. The task of examining budget estimates for conformance with procedures and regulations [3] is unlikely to change due to the rigid nature of public sector auditing requirements.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, budget analysts in specific government contexts may shift toward more complex cost-benefit modeling for payroll adjustments or digital program justification.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For analysts in the aforementioned government settings, if current trajectories of wage experimentation and digital benefit quantification hold, the scope of analysis may expand to include external performance indicators. Extrapolating from municipal wage initiatives, some analysts could be required to analyze data beyond internal records to determine if increased public sector wages are driving local economic growth [1][3]. In settings using digital benefit frameworks, providing technical assistance with cost analysis and fiscal allocation [3] may become conditional on the demonstrated realization of quantified digital benefits [2]. Despite these shifts, the requirement to match appropriations for specific programs with broader program funds [3] will likely persist due to the structural persistence of government funding silos.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, budget analysts in these settings could integrate external socio-economic or program-specific benefit metrics into their budget preparation and fiscal allocation processes.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For budget analysts in municipal and government contexts, long-term evolution depends on the proven efficacy of evidence-based funding models. One plausible outcome is that the role shifts toward strategic fiscal advisory, focusing on the socio-economic impact of budget allocations [1][3] and the long-term ROI of digital infrastructure [2]. A rival outcome exists where fiscal volatility leads to a return to strict expenditure controls, reducing growth modeling in favor of austerity. A primary unknown is whether public sector payrolls and digital investments can be sustainably decoupled from immediate tax increases. Regardless of the scenario, the task of testifying before fund-granting authorities [3] will likely resist change because of the requirement for human political accountability.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the role may evolve into a strategic fiscal advisor focusing on the socio-economic and programmatic impacts of budget allocations.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the role may revert to a strict compliance and austerity function focused on expenditure control.*

title: Credit Analysts
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of workers in the mortgage and agricultural lending subsegments, and for analysts at foreign banks operating in China, operational workflows are shaped by fragmented technology and shifting regulatory ratios. In mortgage lending, workflow fragmentation creates an "interoperability tax" that increases manual effort when completing loan applications and preparing reports that include the degree of risk [1]. This friction persists because disparate systems fail to exchange data, forcing analysts to manually synthesize information [1]. Simultaneously, legacy underwriting logic in mortgage tools limits the impact of automation on how analysts verify income and assess risk [2]. For analysts at foreign banks in China, the task of analyzing credit data to determine risk is currently being adjusted to incorporate raised overseas-loan leverage ratios mandated by the PBOC [4]. In agricultural lending, early AI investments may begin to alter the process of analyzing credit data and financial statements [3]. The task of consulting with customers to resolve complaints and verify financial transactions is unlikely to change, as it requires real-time interpersonal negotiation that resists current systemic automation [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, credit analysts in specialized subsegments may face a paradox of increased AI investment alongside persistent manual burdens caused by poor data interoperability and legacy verification logic.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For a subset of workers in the mortgage and agricultural lending subsegments, and those operating under the PBOC regulatory framework, the operational burden may shift if data standardization and AI scaling hold. If industry-wide interoperability standards are adopted in mortgage lending, the manual effort associated with completing loan applications may decrease, potentially shifting analyst focus toward generating financial ratios to evaluate customers' financial status [1]. Extrapolating from current trajectories in agricultural lending, AI tools may move from experimental pilots to standard components of analyzing financial data to determine expected profitability [3]. For analysts evaluating Chinese outbound investment, risk models may become more standardized around PBOC leverage ratios, reducing the need for ad-hoc ratio calculations [4]. The process of reviewing individual or commercial customer files to identify delinquent accounts is likely to persist unchanged, as it requires situational judgment regarding borrower distress that remains highly variable [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, provided that data interoperability and AI scaling occur, analysts in these subsegments may shift from manual data aggregation toward higher-level risk synthesis.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For a subset of workers in the mortgage and agricultural lending subsegments, and those in the China-linked lending market, long-term resolution of data fragmentation leads to rival outcomes. In one scenario, the elimination of interoperability barriers and the maturity of AI risk engines render the manual portion of summarizing loan requests and preparing risk reports obsolete [1][3]. In a competing scenario, the continued proliferation of proprietary, niche-specific tools maintains a baseline of fragmentation, requiring analysts to function as human integrators who reconcile data between specialized systems [1]. It remains unknown whether the economic incentives of proprietary vendor ecosystems will eventually be superseded by open data standards [1]. The final determination of risk for high-value or complex loans, including large-scale outbound investments, will likely resist change because the catastrophic error cost of systemic lending failures necessitates human accountability [2][4].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, unified data ecosystems and mature AI risk engines may render manual report preparation and loan summarization obsolete for these subsegments.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, persistent tool fragmentation may lock analysts into a role of human data integrators who manually bridge proprietary system gaps.*

title: Financial and Investment Analysts
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For financial and investment analysts broadly, the task of interpreting data on price, yield, and stability is increasingly constrained by high-frequency geopolitical volatility [1][3]. For a subset of workers performing startup diligence, the increase in AI funding requires that assessing companies as investments now include technical auditing of model integrity and training protocols [4]. In the banking subsegment, analysts who analyze the operational performance of companies are focusing on revenue resilience to determine if large-scale technology investments are sustainable [2]. For analysts specializing in proxy advisory, new regulatory guidance may alter the task of recommending investments by imposing fiduciary duty standards on their advice [6]. In certain M&A contexts, the process of performing securities valuation or pricing may prioritize corporate scale over geopolitical risks [5]. The task of collaborating on projects with other professionals, such as lawyers or accountants, is unlikely to change because the legal and tax complexities of transaction execution still require human-centric verification [7].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the occupation may shift toward incorporating technical AI performance audits and fiduciary compliance for proxy services into standard investment analysis.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For analysts in high-growth technology and banking settings, if current trajectories of AI investment and geopolitical instability hold, the task of informing investment decisions may depend on the continuous synthesis of high-frequency, unstructured data streams [1][3]. Extrapolating from current diligence trends, the ability to audit the technical integrity of AI models could become a standard requirement when evaluating and comparing the relative quality of various securities [4][5]. The task of developing and maintaining client relationships persists unchanged because the high-stakes nature of investment capital relies on interpersonal trust and institutional reputation [7].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, technical AI auditing may evolve from a specialty skill into a core competency for analysts assessing high-growth technology sectors.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For analysts in these high-growth or volatile contexts, rival outcomes exist regarding the role of human synthesis in valuation. One scenario involves the displacement of human interpretation of geopolitical and technical signals by automated systems, leaving humans to act as final validators for asset allocation [1][4]. A competing scenario suggests that the high error cost of geopolitical miscalculation and the opacity of complex AI systems will preserve the requirement for human analysts to develop plans of action for investment [3]. It remains unknown whether algorithmic models can reconcile contradictory signals—such as simultaneous market rallies and deteriorating macroeconomic fundamentals—without human intervention. The task of advising clients on aspects of capitalization will likely resist change due to its dependence on negotiated constraints and fiduciary trust [7].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, automated systems may handle the majority of data interpretation for geopolitical and technical signals, with humans acting as final risk validators.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, human analysts may be specifically retained for their capacity to interpret nuanced, unstructured political and technical signals that resist quantification.*

title: Personal Financial Advisors
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For the occupation broadly, the integration of financial planning capabilities into general-purpose AI agents may shift the initial stage of recommending strategies in investment planning toward automated synthesis [3]. In retail banking settings, the deployment of AI account managers may automate the task of answering clients' questions about the details of financial plans for standardized products [1]. Within large-scale wealth management organizations, AI tools designed to reduce administrative labor may accelerate the process of analyzing financial information obtained from clients by automating data consolidation [2]. Consequently, the task of preparing or interpreting investment performance reports may shift from manual drafting to the verification of AI-generated summaries [2]. However, interviewing clients to determine risk tolerance and financial objectives is unlikely to change yet, as these tasks depend on high social perceptiveness and the assessment of subjective, unstructured psychological drivers [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, AI will automate routine data synthesis and basic client inquiries, particularly in retail banking and large-scale wealth management, reducing the manual labor associated with report preparation.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For a subset of workers in retail banking and large-scale wealth management, if current trajectories in automated data synthesis hold, AI may extend into guiding clients in the gathering of information [2][3]. This shift is plausible if agents can autonomously categorize fragmented records such as bank statements and tax returns with high reliability. This may reduce the time advisors spend on the manual intake of client documentation. The task of meeting with clients' other advisors, such as attorneys or trust officers, is likely to persist unchanged because it requires navigating unstandardized professional relationships and case-specific legal nuances that resist algorithmic modeling [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the administrative burden of client data collection for advisors in large institutions may decrease as AI agents automate the gathering and organization of financial records.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For a subset of workers in retail banking and large-scale wealth management, the transition from AI-supported synthesis to autonomous decision-making depends on the resolution of fiduciary accountability. If regulatory frameworks evolve to permit algorithmic liability, AI may move from suggesting strategies to actively managing client portfolios and keeping plans up-to-date for low-complexity accounts [3]. Conversely, if fiduciary law continues to mandate human accountability for every specific recommendation, AI will remain a sophisticated data-processing layer. It remains unknown whether the commoditization of technical financial analysis will alter the mechanisms advisors use to recruit and maintain client bases [3]. The necessity of managing high-emotion client reactions during market volatility will likely resist change even at this horizon.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, AI may autonomously manage portfolios for a subset of retail banking clients, shifting the human advisor's role toward high-level behavioral coaching.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, strict regulatory requirements for human fiduciary responsibility may prevent AI from moving beyond administrative support, regardless of technical capability.*

title: Insurance Underwriters
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For insurance underwriters broadly, and specifically for those in marine and commercial segments, new risk exclusions and automation tools are altering the execution of core tasks. Because some carriers are retreating from covering AI-generated outputs [3], underwriters may increase the frequency of declining excessive risks [2] for applicants utilizing AI in internal operations. For underwriters in geopolitical high-risk corridors, the expansion of sovereign reinsurance guarantees may lower the threshold for risk acceptance [1], altering the process of authorizing reinsurance of policy when risk is high [7]. In commercial lines and aerospace underwriting, the deployment of specialized platforms may accelerate the task of examining documents to determine degree of risk [1] by automating data ingestion [2]. However, the final decision to decline excessive risks [2] for high-limit, bespoke policies is unlikely to change due to the catastrophic financial cost of a single mispriced high-limit policy.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, underwriters may increasingly implement AI-related exclusions while those in specialized marine and commercial segments shift toward managing risk-offset parameters and automated aggregates.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For insurance underwriters in these same contexts, extrapolating from current trajectories, risk assessment may shift toward systemic analysis of technological and political volatility. If the trend of excluding AI outputs persists [3], the task of evaluating possibility of losses due to catastrophe [4] may expand to include the systemic failure of AI-driven internal processes as a primary risk category. In commercial and aerospace lines, if specialized platforms scale [2], the underwriter's role may move toward refining the rating and specifying applicable endorsements [6] for the automated model's logic rather than reviewing individual documents. The requirement to write to field representatives or medical personnel to obtain further information [3] will likely persist, as nuanced, non-digitized situational data remains necessary to validate the boundaries of automated covers.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the role may transition from primary asset reviewer to a supervisor of automated rating parameters and a validator of AI-related risk exclusions.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For underwriters in these segments, long-term structural outcomes depend on the stability of sovereign risk-offsets and the predictability of AI-driven systemic risks. One possible outcome is the emergence of a standardized framework where underwriting for strategic corridors and complex commercial portfolios becomes a primarily administrative validation process [1][2]. A rival outcome is a return to high-touch, manual underwriting if sovereign guarantees are withdrawn or if AI-driven concentrations lead to systemic collapses that render automated models obsolete [3]. It remains unknown whether automated systems can eventually model the volatility of geopolitical conflict with enough precision to remove human oversight from the authorization of reinsurance [7]. Even in highly automated scenarios, the core mandate to decline risks that exceed total available capital reserves [2] will resist change to prevent total insolvency.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, underwriting for high-risk corridors and complex commercial assets may evolve into a standardized administrative process of verifying compliance with pre-set risk frameworks.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, a systemic failure of AI-driven risk modeling may force a return to manual, high-touch underwriting to manage unquantifiable technological volatility.*

title: Financial Risk Specialists
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For this occupation broadly, the shift of cybersecurity into the remit of chief financial officers requires specialists to analyze areas of potential risk to assets by integrating cyber-exposure into financial liability models [3]. For a subset of workers managing energy and East Asian equity portfolios, geopolitical volatility in the Middle East necessitates more frequent updates to scenario analyses reflecting possible severe market events [1][2][5]. In the banking subsegment, the deployment of high-capability AI models requires specialists to develop or implement risk-assessment models specifically designed to mitigate systemic operational and cyber risks [7][8][9]. In digital currency hubs testing sovereign-backed stablecoins, as seen in Switzerland [6], specialists must develop risk-assessment models to monitor asset peg stability. In maritime risk settings, the expansion of state-backed reinsurance guarantees for critical transit corridors, such as the Strait of Hormuz [4], alters the mechanism used to recommend ways to control or reduce risk by transferring a portion of market volatility to sovereign entities. In regions where central banks raise leverage ratios for foreign lenders, as seen in China [10], specialists must devise systems or processes to monitor the validity of risk assessments regarding increased outbound investment exposure. In organizations using AI for internal processes, the tendency of insurance carriers to decline coverage for AI outputs [11] requires specialists to recommend ways to control or reduce risk through internal capital reserves rather than external risk transfer. The requirement to conduct statistical analyses to quantify risk is unlikely to change because the mathematical foundations of probability and variance remain invariant regardless of the risk source [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, financial risk specialists will integrate cyber-exposure into liability models, develop mitigation frameworks for AI-driven systemic risk in banking, and adjust risk-transfer strategies as insurance coverage for AI outputs diminishes.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For this occupation broadly, if current trajectories of CFO-led risk integration hold, the task of producing reports that outline findings may shift from qualitative descriptions to the use of standardized, quantitative cyber-risk metrics [3]. For the banking subsegment, extrapolating from current AI model risks, the focus may shift from initial risk identification to devising systems or processes to monitor the validity of AI-driven risk assessments [7][8][9]. In maritime risk settings, the continued reliance on state-backed reinsurance may shift the task of analyzing market price volatility toward evaluating the relative quality and creditworthiness of sovereign guarantees [4]. For specialists in digital currency hubs, the transition from stablecoin testing to deployment may require more rigorous efforts to maintain the input or data quality of risk management systems to ensure collateral transparency [6]. In regions utilizing high-leverage foreign lending frameworks [10], the focus may shift toward analyzing the long-term impact of leverage on the earning capacity of foreign lenders. For organizations using AI, the persistent lack of insurance for AI outputs may shift the focus of risk assessment toward the technical auditing of AI models to prevent catastrophic financial loss [11]. The fundamental necessity to gather risk-related data from internal and external resources remains a constant constraint [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may see the standardization of cyber-risk metrics and a shift toward sovereign-credit analysis for specialists in state-insured corridors and digital asset environments.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For this occupation broadly, the trajectory of risk modeling depends on whether systemic geopolitical and AI-driven shocks become predictable parameters or remain exceptional outliers. One plausible outcome is that these risks are absorbed into automated risk management systems, reducing the need for manual intervention in scenario development [3][7][8][9]. A rival outcome is that the increasing complexity of intertwined AI-driven markets creates "black swan" events that resist quantification, maintaining the necessity for bespoke human judgment in identifying key risks [11]. In maritime and sovereign risk settings, the long-term stability of state-backed guarantees remains an unknown variable that could either standardize or destabilize risk-transfer mechanisms [4]. Even at this horizon, the requirement to interpret data on price, yield, and stability resists full automation because the socio-political drivers of market sentiment remain unstructured [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, financial risk specialists in highly automated environments may transition from active model development to the oversight of automated systemic risk monitors.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the unpredictability of AI-generated market shocks may increase the demand for specialists capable of non-linear, qualitative risk synthesis.*

title: Financial Examiners
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For financial examiners broadly, the establishment of specialized task forces to create rules for AI and prediction markets [5] requires a shift in how they review and analyze new laws to determine their impact [O*NET Task 12] and establish guidelines for policies that comply with these regulations [O*NET Task 11]. For a subset of examiners specializing in AI governance, the proposal for audit-ready controls [2] may alter the process of evaluating data processing applications [O*NET Task 14] and reviewing audit reports to discover weaknesses in internal routines [O*NET Task 8]. In the consumer lending subsegment, the movement by the CFPB to narrow civil rights protections [1] may change how examiners recommend actions to ensure compliance [O*NET Task 2] by reducing the scope of fair-lending audits. For those overseeing digital assets, the adoption of "regulator-in-the-loop" strategies [4] may shift the investigation of activities to ensure the legality of transactions [O*NET Task 5] toward more integrated, continuous oversight. For examiners overseeing OCC-regulated institutions, the preemption of state-level interchange laws [6] requires updating examination protocols and checklists to verify that federal preemption is correctly applied [O*NET Task 11]. For examiners reviewing institutions with high technology infrastructure exposure, FASB's monitoring of data center trends [3] may lead to updated methods for reviewing balance sheets to confirm institution assets [O*NET Task 6]. Verifying and inspecting cash reserves and assigned collateral [O*NET Task 16] is unlikely to change because the requirement for objective, third-party physical or hard-asset verification remains a binding constraint.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, examiners broadly will integrate AI and prediction market rules into their workflows, while specific subsegments will adapt to narrowed fair-lending metrics, "regulator-in-the-loop" digital asset oversight, and updated federal preemption protocols.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For financial examiners in these specific subsegments, the nature of compliance verification may shift if current trajectories hold. Extrapolating from the push for audit-ready AI controls [2], the process of investigating activities to ensure legality [O*NET Task 5] may shift from manual transaction sampling toward the validation of automated control logs. In the consumer lending subsegment, the specific actions recommended to ensure compliance [O*NET Task 2] may become more focused on narrow technical binary markers if civil rights protections remain contracted [1]. For those overseeing digital assets, the "regulator-in-the-loop" model [4] could evolve into a standardized requirement for real-time data access, altering the timing and frequency of investigating operations [O*NET Task 5]. The reporting of data center financing may move from a monitored trend to a standardized accounting requirement, altering the documentation used to confirm institution assets [O*NET Task 6]. However, the requirement to direct and participate in formal meetings with bank directors and senior management to discuss findings [O*NET Task 1] will likely persist, as the communication of regulatory failure and institutional accountability requires human-mediated negotiation and professional judgment.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, specialized examiner toolkits may transition toward the verification of automated governance logs and real-time data streams rather than periodic retrospective audits.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For examiners in these subsegments, long-term outcomes depend on whether regulatory frameworks stabilize or fragment. If "audit-ready" controls [2] and "regulator-in-the-loop" strategies [4] become the universal standard, the evaluation of data processing applications [O*NET Task 14] may become a highly automated process of algorithmic verification. A rival outcome is a fragmented landscape where diverging state and federal interpretations of preemption [6] and civil rights [1] create conflicting compliance requirements, increasing the complexity of establishing guidelines for procedures [O*NET Task 11]. One major unknown is the legal status of autonomous agents in financial transactions and whether they can be held accountable under existing solvency laws. Despite these shifts, the final determination of an institution's safety and soundness [O*NET Task 3] will resist full automation due to the high error cost and the necessity of human legal liability in regulatory sign-offs.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the role of the examiner in high-tech subsegments may shift toward a systems auditor who validates the integrity of the automated regulatory loop.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the role may shift toward a conflict mediator who resolves contradictions between fragmented jurisdictional mandates and automated institutional reports.*

title: Loan Officers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For mortgage lenders, small-volume lenders, agricultural lenders, and banking organizations adopting agentic AI, automated systems may reduce the manual effort required for explaining to customers the different types of loans and credit options [1][6]. In small-volume lending settings, streamlined credit report access may automate the process of obtaining and compiling copies of loan applicants' credit histories [5]. Within mortgage-specific contexts, the reduction of workflow fragmentation through software interoperability could accelerate the task of reviewing loan agreements to ensure they are complete and accurate [3]. A "verification-first" shift in mortgage lending may alter the mechanism of analyzing applicants' financial status by prioritizing raw income verification over traditional debt-to-income ratios [4]. For agricultural lenders deploying AI pilots, automated workflows may streamline the process of analyzing financial status to determine the feasibility of granting loans [8]. Narrowing civil rights protections in U.S. federal lending rules may modify the compliance parameters used when analyzing applicants' financial status [2]. For lenders in China, the increase in leverage ratios for foreign banks may alter the process of approving loans within specified limits to support outbound investment [9]. For the occupation broadly, loan officers must increasingly manage borrower hesitation by debunking market myths to advise on the timing of loans [7]. The task of approving loans outside specified limits is unlikely to change yet because institutional risk thresholds and senior-level accountability remain centralized [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, AI agents and improved digital onboarding tools will likely reduce the administrative burden of data gathering and initial client education for a subset of loan officers, while the broader role will focus more on guiding borrowers through market volatility.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For a subset of workers in integrated or AI-adopting organizations, if current trajectories in borrower-side AI agency hold, the task of meeting with applicants to obtain information may shift toward managing data exchanges between competing agentic systems [6]. Extrapolating from the narrowing of civil rights protections, the legal risk associated with algorithmic credit scoring may decrease, potentially shifting a larger portion of analyzing applicants' financial status to automated systems [2]. The human role may shift toward resolving mortgage application problems that require high-level negotiation or complex exception handling [4]. However, handling customer complaints is likely to persist as a human-led task because the social perceptiveness required to resolve interpersonal disputes exceeds current agentic capabilities [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, for those in integrated settings, the review and verification of loan files may become largely automated, shifting the human role toward managing complex exceptions and interpersonal disputes.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For workers in organizations using integrated AI account systems and operating under shifting regulatory regimes, the long-term distribution of decision authority remains unknown. One possibility is that fully integrated workflows and AI managers perform the primary analysis of financial status, restricting human intervention to approving loans outside specified limits for high-risk exceptions [1][3]. A competing possibility is that a regulatory reversal reinstating strict antidiscrimination requirements may mandate human-led auditing of all credit decisions to mitigate systemic bias, limiting the role of AI to data preparation [2]. It remains unknown whether the negotiating power shift toward borrower agents will lead to a complete commoditization of loan terms. The physical act of meeting with applicants in person may resist change for ultra-high-net-worth commercial lending where trust is based on personal relationship networks rather than algorithmic verification.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, for workers in highly automated firms, the loan officer role may be reduced to a final risk-governance function for non-standard loan approvals.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, for workers in strictly regulated regimes, the loan officer role may expand into a mandatory compliance and ethics auditor for all automated credit decisions.*

title: Tax Examiners and Collectors, and Revenue Agents
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of workers in national revenue agencies, such as the US Internal Revenue Service, the operational capacity to notify taxpayers of any overpayment or underpayment and enter tax return information into computers may depend on the availability of supplemental legislative funds, such as those from the Inflation Reduction Act [2]. For revenue agents in the United Kingdom, the processes of reviewing filed tax returns to determine if deductions are allowed and collecting taxes from businesses involve applying technical guidance from the National Minimum Wage Manual and the Employment Income Manual [3][4]. Specifically, for agents in Northern Ireland, legislative changes under the Customs (Northern Ireland) (EU Exit) (Amendment) Regulations 2026 alter the mechanism for approving repayment or remission of Customs Duty for businesses bringing goods into the region [5]. In jurisdictions where prediction markets are legally contested, as reported in New Hampshire and other US states, the requirement to maintain knowledge of tax code changes increases as these platforms introduce new forms of taxable wagering [1]. The authority to direct service of legal documents, such as subpoenas or warrants, is unlikely to change because it is derived from statutory mandates rather than administrative funding or emerging market trends [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, operational stability in some national agencies may fluctuate based on supplemental funding, while agents in specific regions must adapt to new customs regulations and emerging digital revenue sources.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For organizations such as the US Internal Revenue Service, if current trajectories of reliance on supplemental grants continue, the ability to review selected tax returns to determine the nature of audits may be sensitive to periodic appropriation cycles [2]. In jurisdictions where prediction markets have been codified, extrapolating from current legal disputes suggests agents may spend more time examining accounting systems and records to verify that digital platform computations comply with statutory provisions [1]. This shift assumes these jurisdictions successfully establish tax obligations for prediction markets without federal preemption. The requirement to confer with taxpayers or their representatives to resolve problems with returns persists unchanged because the resolution of disputes depends on human judgment of individual circumstances and negotiation [3].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, enforcement capacity in some national agencies could remain volatile, while agents in affected regions may increase specialized auditing of digital market entities.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For organizations such as the US Internal Revenue Service, the long-term stability of the collection pipeline depends on whether funding models shift from supplemental grants to permanent structural appropriations [2]. For agents in jurisdictions that successfully regulate prediction markets, as reported in New Hampshire and other US states, one plausible outcome is that they integrate these digital assets into procedures for investigating claims of inability to pay taxes [1][4]. A competing outcome is that persistent legal ambiguity regarding digital markets prevents standardized collection, leaving agents reliant on traditional asset classes [1]. It remains unknown whether initial IT investments funded by the Inflation Reduction Act will eventually eliminate the need for the manual entry of tax return information into computers [2]. The determination of appropriate methods of debt settlement, such as wage garnishment or seizure of property, resists change due to the inherent legal requirements for due process and judicial oversight.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, revenue agents in regulated jurisdictions integrate digital prediction market assets into standard asset investigation and collection workflows.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, persistent legal ambiguity surrounding digital prediction markets prevents the standardization of collection, forcing agents to rely on traditional financial asset classes.*

title: Tax Preparers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For tax preparers broadly, the deployment of AI agents capable of drafting tax returns [3][4] shifts the task of preparing simple to complex tax returns [2] from manual composition to the verification of machine-generated drafts. In regions with standardized digital government guidance, such as for National Insurance contributions and Construction Industry Scheme refunds in the United Kingdom [1][2], the task of computing taxes owed or overpaid [2] is increasingly facilitated by government-provided calculation logic. For tax preparers in settings utilizing mobile-integrated AI agents [5], the task of interviewing clients to obtain taxable income and deductible expenses [4] may be partially shifted to asynchronous, AI-driven data collection via messaging platforms. The task of explaining federal and state tax laws to individuals and companies [8] is unlikely to change in the near term because the high error cost of legal misinterpretation requires a licensed professional to provide the final interpretive authority.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, tax preparers will transition from primary drafters to editors of AI-generated returns, while those in digitally advanced jurisdictions will rely more on government-provided calculation tools for specific liability schemes.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For tax preparers broadly, if the adoption of AI drafting agents continues, the task of reviewing financial records to determine needed forms [6] may shift toward an audit-style verification of AI-categorized data. For preparers in regions with integrated digital tax infrastructure, the task of consulting tax law handbooks for atypical returns [10] may be reduced for standardized schemes as the logic is embedded directly into the drafting agents [1][2]. However, the task of checking data input to detect errors in arithmetic or procedure [7] persists because the legal liability for the accuracy of the filing remains with the human preparer. The requirement to furnish taxpayers with advice to ensure correct tax form completion [3] remains necessary to manage the boundary between legal tax minimization and non-compliance.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the core value of the tax preparer shifts from the technical execution of return preparation to the legal certification and risk management of automated outputs.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For tax preparers broadly, the possibility of real-time state-led data reconciliation introduces rival outcomes. If governments implement systems where credits and deductions are applied automatically at the point of transaction, the task of preparing simple tax returns [5] and claiming refunds [1] may be eliminated. Conversely, if financial instruments and corporate layering increase in complexity, the task of reviewing financial records to determine forms [6] may resist further automation. It remains unknown whether state-led automation will encompass all atypical returns or if a permanent niche for high-complexity manual synthesis will persist. Even at this horizon, the task of calculating form preparation fees according to complexity [11] remains a business-level pricing decision resistant to technical automation.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, real-time government reconciliation and AI drafting eliminate the need for human intervention in the majority of individual and small business tax filings.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, increasing complexity in global financial instruments and corporate layering preserves the necessity for human preparers to manually synthesize records and trigger complex claims.*

title: Financial Quantitative Analysts
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of quantitative analysts operating in AI-driven prediction markets and regulated financial settings, the emergence of specific regulatory "rules of the road" creates a binding constraint on model development [2]. Because the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) is actively establishing frameworks for AI-driven novel products, the task of defining model specifications or data collection methods [O*NET 5] must now incorporate explicit regulatory compliance mechanisms [2]. In these high-stakes environments, the specific judgment of the human developer acts as a "moat," meaning the task of maintaining or modifying financial analytic models [O*NET 7] depends on human expertise to prevent catastrophic "black box" errors that would trigger regulatory penalties [1]. The task of producing written summary reports [O*NET 6] is unlikely to change significantly yet, as these documents serve as the essential evidentiary trail for regulatory accountability.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, for analysts in regulated AI-driven prediction markets, the ability to align model construction with emerging regulatory mandates will be the primary competitive advantage.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the same subset of workers in regulated AI-first settings, the role may shift toward the formal auditing of AI-generated tools if current trajectories hold [1]. Extrapolating from the move toward structured AI prediction market rules [2], the task of devising independent models to verify results [O*NET 9] could evolve into a primary regulatory function to ensure autonomous systems remain within legal bounds [2]. The fundamental requirement for applying mathematical or statistical techniques [O*NET 1] will persist unchanged, as these provide the only objective basis for validating the outputs of autonomous analytical tools against market reality.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupational focus for this subsegment may pivot from primary model construction toward the regulatory verification and auditing of AI-generated quantitative tools.*

## Far (2046–2051)

Within regulated AI-first financial contexts, the role of the analyst may diverge based on the maturity of automated oversight [1][2]. One possibility is that analysts evolve into systemic architects who focus on the high-level task of defining model specifications [O*NET 5] for fleets of autonomous systems, emphasizing the structural integrity of the financial pipeline [1]. A rival outcome is that the standardization of AI regulatory protocols [2] commoditizes the "human moat," reducing the specialized value of the individual builder. It remains unknown whether regulatory bodies will ever permit the fully autonomous valuation of complex instruments without a legally accountable human signatory. The fundamental task of interpreting results of financial analysis procedures [O*NET 3] will likely resist change, as fiduciary responsibility for catastrophic loss requires a human agent.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, analysts in this subsegment may evolve into system architects who govern and certify the behavior of autonomous quantitative model fleets.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the standardization of AI regulatory audits may erode the specialized value of the human builder, commoditizing the task of model development.*

title: Fraud Examiners, Investigators and Analysts
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For fraud examiners broadly, the emergence of synthetic corporate identities may alter the process of gathering financial documents related to investigations [1]. Because state-sponsored actors can pose as legitimate trading firms to execute high-value thefts, the task of analyzing financial data to detect irregularities can no longer assume the authenticity of registered corporate entities [1]. In regions where attackers employ SEO poisoning and Adversary-in-the-Middle tactics to redirect salary payments, the process of reviewing reports of suspected fraud may shift toward analyzing external search-result manipulation [3]. For a subsegment of examiners managing agentic commerce and expense management, the task of analyzing financial data to detect irregularities shifts from monitoring human behavioral patterns to identifying agent-hijacking or automated expense anomalies [4][6]. For a subsegment of examiners focusing on banking security, identifying irregularities may shift toward detecting signatures of illicit bypass tools sold on encrypted platforms [5]. The focus of designing, implementing, or maintaining fraud detection tools may shift toward network-level deterrence to make the fraud ecosystem less attractive to attackers [2]. The task of interviewing witnesses or suspects and taking statements is unlikely to change, as the detection of human deception remains an interpersonal process resistant to digital automation [1].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, fraud examiners will shift from verifying the presence of documentation to verifying the operational legitimacy of the entities providing that documentation.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For fraud examiners broadly, if current trajectories of state-sponsored synthetic identity fabrication hold, the task of coordinating investigative efforts with law enforcement officers and attorneys may be constrained by the geopolitical protections afforded to the creators of these entities [1]. Extrapolating from the scale of losses in synthetic entity fraud, the process of reviewing reports of suspected fraud to determine the need for further investigation may transition toward a triage system based on the suspected sovereign origin of the attacker [1]. For a subsegment of examiners overseeing agentic commerce, the baseline for "normal" financial behavior may become more volatile if AI-driven transaction volumes mask illicit flows [4]. The core requirement to prepare evidence for presentation in court persists unchanged because legal standards for the admissibility of evidence are governed by judicial precedent rather than technological capacity [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may integrate geopolitical intelligence into the investigative workflow to identify and track state-sponsored financial crime.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For fraud examiners broadly, the structural nature of the role may diverge based on the technical equilibrium between generative fraud and automated verification. If synthetic corporate histories become indistinguishable from organic ones, the task of analyzing financial data to detect irregularities may shift from proactive detection to reactive recovery and loss mitigation [1][2]. A primary uncertainty remains whether a universal "proof of entity" standard can be implemented to neutralize AI-fabricated identities. The requirement to testify in court regarding investigation findings resists change even at this horizon, as the legal system's reliance on a human agent to be held accountable for testimony is a fundamental structural constraint [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may shift primarily toward reactive loss recovery as proactive detection of synthetic identities becomes computationally improbable.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may evolve into a verification-auditing role centered on managing a universal, cryptographically secured proof-of-entity infrastructure.*

title: Computer Systems Analysts
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For the occupation broadly, analysts are increasingly performing AI mapping to align technical model capabilities with specific business requirements to improve revenue outcomes [2]. In organizations transitioning to agentic workflows, the task of expanding or modifying systems to improve work flow shifts from designing static automation to agent-first process redesign [4]. Broadly, the task of preparing cost-benefit and return-on-investment analyses is being altered by a transition in total cost of ownership (TCO) metrics toward cost-per-token as the primary KPI for AI infrastructure [7]. For analysts in public sector environments, the task of planning and designing computer systems must now account for specific operational constraints and governance mandates [6]. In smart manufacturing settings, coordinating and linking computer systems now involves integrating Internet of Things (IoT) data with customer relationship management platforms [1]. For a subset of workers in corporate administration, assessing the usefulness of pre-developed application packages includes implementing AI-powered onboarding agents [3]. In organizations using cloud-based AI projects, analysts may use new attribution tools to manage inference costs [5]. The task of troubleshooting program and system malfunctions is unlikely to change significantly because the initial diagnostic phase for hardware or low-level system failures remains a manual, technical process [8].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, analysts broadly will shift toward mapping AI capabilities to business outcomes and redesigning processes for autonomous agents, while subsegments in manufacturing, government, and cloud operations integrate specialized agentic and cost-tracking tools.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the occupation broadly, if current trajectories in agent-first design hold, analysts may transition from initial process mapping to the continuous optimization of dynamic systems that adapt in real time [4]. Extrapolating from current integration patterns in smart manufacturing, analysts in that subsegment could expand or modify systems to enable autonomous, closed-loop predictive maintenance [1]. In administrative subsegments, the focus may shift from building single-purpose agents to managing ecosystems of interconnected lifecycle agents [3]. For analysts in cloud-native environments, the ability to track granular inference costs could evolve from retrospective analysis to real-time resource reallocation [5]. The task of consulting with management to ensure agreement on system principles will persist because the governance of autonomous agent behavior requires human negotiation regarding organizational risk and accountability [8].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, analysts may transition from designing static system architectures to managing the evolutionary behavior and economic efficiency of autonomous agent ecosystems.*

## Far (2046–2051)

Scope is limited to organizations where agentic orchestration and high-frequency data integration are central to the business model. One plausible outcome is that analysts continue to define the goals of the system and devise logical operational steps to manage the high-level orchestration of multi-agent systems, as business logic remains too heterogeneous for total automation [4]. A rival outcome exists if AI mapping tools evolve to autonomously bridge the gap between business needs and technical implementation, reducing the analyst's role in the initial design phase [2]. It remains unknown whether the mapping function will persist as a distinct human activity or be absorbed into a software self-configuration layer. The task of interviewing or surveying workers to determine how information is processed will resist change because capturing tacit, uncodified human expertise requires social interaction that agents cannot replicate [8].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, analysts remain essential for high-level orchestration and the definition of system goals within complex, heterogeneous business environments.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the role of the analyst in system design is significantly diminished as AI mapping tools automate the alignment of business needs with technical architecture.*

title: Health Informatics Specialists
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For health informatics specialists broadly, the task of designing or implementing health information technology applications is shifting toward the integration of AI-driven platforms for hospital operations [3]. In organizations deploying patient-facing chatbots to maintain control over health information, the task of selecting and evaluating informatics solutions now requires validating the clinical safety of these interfaces [4][5]. For a subset of workers in organizations implementing generative AI, the task of translating nursing practice information between nurses and engineers involves the specific refinement of model prompts to align with clinical workflows [1]. In regions where state governments are regulating chatbot usage, the task of developing policies for patient information security may be altered by new requirements for algorithmic safety audits [2]. In organizations facing AI scalability bottlenecks, the task of evaluating health information technology structures now involves modifying the underlying data architecture to support AI deployment [6]. The task of troubleshooting telehealth technology in homes is unlikely to change because it requires physical intervention and site-specific hardware configuration [7].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the occupation may shift toward managing AI-driven operational logistics and the safety validation of patient-facing chatbots.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For health informatics specialists broadly, if current regulatory trajectories hold, the task of developing strategies for modifying information technology may evolve into a cycle of auditing algorithmic outputs to satisfy state-level mandates [2]. Extrapolating from early generative AI implementations, the task of delivering training programs for health information technology could expand to include specialized curricula for detecting hallucinations in clinical data [1]. The task of providing consultation to nurses regarding hardware configuration is likely to persist unchanged because the physical infrastructure of medical devices remains fragmented and requires localized support [7].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, this role may formalize as a clinical AI governor, balancing operational efficiency with state-mandated safety compliance.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For health informatics specialists in high-automation settings, the role's evolution depends on whether algorithmic certification replaces the need for human-led policy modification. In one scenario, the role further specializes into a regulatory auditing function focused on the safety of autonomous nursing systems. In a competing scenario, the task of translating nursing practice information between clinical staff and designers may be automated by advanced translation models, reducing the distinct need for this intermediary role. It remains unknown if automated compliance monitors can replace human judgment in the development of security policies. The task of disseminating information about nursing informatics science to the profession is likely to resist change, as professional ethical frameworks are defined through human peer discourse [7].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the subsegment may transition into a specialized regulatory role focused on the certification and auditing of autonomous clinical systems.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may lose its distinct identity as automated tools reduce the need for human intermediaries to bridge nursing practice and system design.*

title: Information Security Analysts
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For information security analysts broadly, because residential proxy networks allow attackers to masquerade as legitimate home users to bypass IP-reputation filters [3], the mechanism for regulating access to safeguard information shifts from IP-based blocking toward behavioral telemetry and identity-based analysis. Because AI-assisted supply chain attacks target open-source repositories [9] and malicious packages are distributed across npm, PyPI, and Go [33], the task of monitoring current reports of computer viruses now requires continuous provenance auditing of third-party software dependencies [9][33]. For a subset of workers in organizations deploying autonomous agents, the process of regulating access to safeguard information now includes auditing and eliminating orphaned non-human identities, such as forgotten API keys and service accounts, which are primary drivers of cloud breaches [86]. For analysts in industrial settings, because state-sponsored actors specifically target PLC and SCADA systems in energy and water infrastructure [24][28], the task of performing risk assessments pivots toward detecting disruptive attacks on operational technology. Because high-capability models like Claude Mythos enable the rapid, autonomous discovery of software vulnerabilities [15][21], the timeline for zero-day threats may collapse, requiring the task of executing tests of data processing systems to move to a near-real-time cadence [22][30][62]. Training users and promoting security awareness is unlikely to change yet because industrialized social engineering continues to exploit human cognitive biases regardless of technical advancements [10][16].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, analysts broadly may transition toward behavioral detection and provenance auditing, while specific subsegments integrate specialized risk intelligence for non-human identities or industrial control systems.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For information security analysts broadly, if the collapse of the zero-day timeline [30] and the rise of agentic attack speeds [22] persist, the task of performing risk assessments may shift from monitoring mean time to detection toward closing the "post-alert gap" via automated remediation workflows [60]. For a subset of workers in highly regulated environments, the task of documenting computer security policies may transition from manual audit logs to using automated reasoning and formal verification to produce mathematically proven compliance results [79]. For workers in organizations deploying autonomous agents, because agent intent is an insufficient security proxy [36], the task of modifying computer security files may pivot toward the real-time governance of agent permissions using specialized governance toolkits [31]. Extrapolating from current quantum computing warnings [82], the mechanism for encrypting data transmissions will likely shift toward the deployment of post-quantum cryptographic standards to maintain confidentiality [43]. Reviewing violations of computer security procedures and discussing them with violators persists as a human-centric task because correcting behavioral errors requires qualitative social judgment and interpersonal negotiation [10].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, analysts broadly may move toward auditing automated agent interactions and remediation speed, while the core of policy enforcement remains anchored in human social judgment.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For information security analysts broadly, the scope of the occupation remains bounded by the persistence of an environment where AI-native models can autonomously discover and exploit vulnerabilities. Because AI-native threat intelligence [44] and defensive models [67][85] may automate the bulk of monitoring current reports of computer viruses and updating virus protection systems, the analyst's role may shift toward the strategic governance of these models. A significant uncertainty remains whether defensive AI can maintain a structural advantage over offensive AI or if the "zero-day" state becomes the permanent baseline. The task of conferring with users to discuss access needs resists automation even at this horizon because it involves negotiating organizational power and operational trade-offs.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may shift toward a high-level governance role, overseeing an automated stalemate where AI defenses and attacks neutralize each other in real-time.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, if AI-generated vulnerabilities outpace remediation, the occupation may shift toward managing extreme isolation and manual air-gapping of critical data systems.*

title: Computer and Information Research Scientists
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For computer and information research scientists broadly, the introduction of architectures reducing energy consumption by 100x [1] and techniques for making models leaner during the learning process [15] may alter how they apply theoretical expertise and innovation to create new technology. Because existing agentic AI benchmarks are considered insufficient [3][4], the task of evaluating work in light of established standards shifts toward the adoption of performance-prediction frameworks [5] and the rigorous determination of minimum rater sufficiency [6]. For a subset of workers in systems architecture, the engineering of gigawatt-scale datacenters [7] and the development of specialized GPU communications on AMD platforms [8] change how they design computers and the software that runs them. For researchers focused on safety and alignment, the need to protect users from harmful manipulation [9] and evaluate behavioral dispositions [10] alters how they conduct logical analyses of technical problems. In resource-constrained nations, as reported in India [14], theoretical expertise may shift toward the creation of frugal models to maintain capability despite compute limitations [13]. Tasks involving the approval and adjustment of operational budgets are unlikely to change, as these remain governed by administrative financial constraints [19].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, researchers broadly will integrate extreme energy-efficiency and synthetic data constraints into their theoretical work, while subsegments in systems architecture, safety, and robotics pivot toward gigawatt-scale infrastructure and grounded behavioral evaluation.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For computer and information research scientists broadly, if current trajectories in decentralized training [16] and on-the-job learning architectures [17] hold, the reduction in the cost of iterative experimentation could shift how they analyze problems to develop solutions involving computer hardware and software. Extrapolating from current research, the process of applying theoretical expertise may move toward the design of systems capable of autonomous architectural refinement. For a subset of workers specializing in quantum computing, the establishment of logical qubit standards [18] may stabilize the mechanisms used to design computers. The requirement to consult with users, management, vendors, and technicians to determine computing needs will persist unchanged because system requirements are fundamentally tied to human organizational objectives [19].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may shift toward the design of self-optimizing architectures, reducing the manual burden of theoretical iteration while increasing the focus on high-level system constraints and standard-setting.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For computer and information research scientists broadly, the trajectory of the occupation depends on whether the field converges on unified standards for integrating divergent computing paradigms. If such standards emerge, the task of designing computers and the software that runs them may shift toward the orchestration of heterogeneous, self-evolving systems. If the field remains fragmented between gigawatt-scale centralized clusters [7] and frugal, decentralized models [13][16], researchers may diverge into distinct specialized roles: scale engineers focused on infrastructure and efficiency theorists focused on algorithmic minimalism. It remains unknown whether alignment and safety constraints can be fully reduced to a set of mathematically formalizable proofs. The fundamental reliance on conducting logical analyses and formulating mathematical models of problems will resist change even at this horizon [19].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation converges on a unified role centered on the orchestration of self-evolving, heterogeneous computing architectures.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation diverges into two distinct specializations based on a permanent structural split between centralized hyper-scale computing and decentralized frugal computing.*

title: Computer User Support Specialists
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For computer user support specialists broadly, the deployment of AI agents within IT service management platforms [3] and the rise of sophisticated helpdesk-targeted phishing [1][2] alter the initial stages of user interaction. Because AI agents are being integrated to handle ticket intake and triage [3], the task of answering user inquiries regarding computer software or hardware operation [2] is partially shifted to automated systems. Simultaneously, the use of fake authentication pages to bypass corporate security [2] forces a shift in how specialists investigate and resolve problems [2], moving from trust-based verification to rigid, multi-factor authentication playbooks [1]. This necessitates more meticulous maintenance of records regarding remedial actions taken [2] to ensure auditability during security incidents. Physical tasks, such as setting up equipment for employee use [2], are unlikely to change due to the requirement for manual cable installation and hardware placement.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the occupation will shift toward a hybrid model where AI agents handle routine triage and human specialists focus on high-stakes identity verification and complex troubleshooting.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For computer user support specialists broadly, if the deployment of AI agents for helpdesk governance continues to scale [3], the process of investigating and resolving problems [2] may move toward a "zero-trust" operational model. In this trajectory, the specialist's role in granting access or resetting credentials is constrained by automated cryptographic verification, reducing human discretion in identity adjudication. This shift may alter how specialists develop training materials for users [2], prioritizing secure identity hygiene over basic software navigation. The need to confer with staff and management to establish requirements for new systems [2] persists because organizational workflows and internal politics remain too idiosyncratic for algorithmic standardization.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, symbolic support tasks may be largely governed by AI agents, leaving human specialists to manage the exceptions and failures of these automated systems.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For computer user support specialists broadly, the trajectory of the occupation may diverge based on the evolution of AI-driven social engineering. In one outcome, symbolic support for software and account access is fully automated, leaving human specialists to focus almost exclusively on performing minor repairs to hardware [2]. In a competing outcome, a "verified human" support tier may emerge for high-security environments where automated identity adjudication is viewed as a vulnerability to advanced AI-driven attacks. It remains unknown whether AI can distinguish between biological human social engineering and synthetic impersonation without excessive false positives. The requirement to inspect equipment and prepare it for delivery to users [2] resists change due to the physical variability of hardware shipments.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may split into a hardware-centric technician role as symbolic support is fully automated.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, human specialists may be retained as a mandatory security layer for high-value identity authentication to counter synthetic social engineering.*

title: Computer Network Architects
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For network architects broadly, the shift in data center utility from general processing to "AI token factories" is altering how they develop conceptual, logical, or physical network designs to prioritize the minimization of latency and cost per token [5]. In regions affected by geopolitical instability, such as Asia and the Gulf, architects are adjusting their approach to developing disaster recovery plans to account for physical strikes on concentrated infrastructure [3][4]. For a subsegment of workers designing hyper-scale AI training clusters, the requirement for multi-gigawatt power envelopes alters the process of determining specific network hardware or software requirements, shifting focus toward proprietary high-speed fabrics and AI-specific interconnects [1][2]. In these high-density environments, adjusting network sizes to meet volume or capacity demands is now constrained by thermal boundaries and energy distribution limits [1][5]. Coordinating the installation of new equipment in these settings requires direct alignment with power infrastructure capable of supporting gigawatt-scale loads [1][2]. Standard local area network designs for administrative office use are unlikely to change significantly because they do not face these extreme power-density or geopolitical concentration pressures [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, network architects will increasingly optimize designs for token-generation efficiency, while a specialized subsegment shifts toward power-constrained interconnect design for massive compute clusters.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For network architects broadly, if current trajectories hold, the process of developing disaster recovery plans may shift from localized redundancy toward systemic regional decoupling to ensure resilience against large-scale infrastructure strikes [3][4]. For the subsegment of hyper-scale infrastructure architects, extrapolating from the emergence of multi-gigawatt sites suggests that physical network design may be increasingly dictated by thermal management and energy distribution limits rather than traditional data throughput alone [1][2]. This could lead to a tighter integration between network architecture and power systems engineering to maintain cluster coherence at scale [1][5]. Core routing protocols for general internet traffic and standard enterprise WANs will likely persist unchanged due to the massive installed base of legacy hardware and global standardization [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may bifurcate between specialists in geopolitically resilient distributed networks and those managing the integrated power-data fabrics of gigawatt-scale compute sites.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For network architects broadly, the tension between the efficiency of centralized gigawatt clusters and the security of geographic diversification remains a primary structural uncertainty [1][3]. It remains unknown whether the field will develop mechanisms for virtual coherence across high-latency distances or if physical site size will reach a hard ceiling due to power and risk constraints [1][2]. One plausible outcome involves the persistence of the gigawatt-site model as the dominant paradigm for large-scale training, accepting higher concentration risk for the benefit of lower latency [1][5]. A rival outcome suggests a forced transition to decentralized, resilient fabrics that prioritize geopolitical survival over raw training speed [3][4]. Basic network-related documentation and troubleshooting procedures for low-complexity, non-AI systems will likely resist change as they rely on stable, low-performance logic [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, network architecture remains centered on increasingly massive, single-site gigawatt clusters, with design focused almost exclusively on extreme-density interconnects.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, network architecture shifts toward highly decentralized, geopolitically fragmented fabrics that sacrifice peak performance for systemic resilience.*
