title: Telecommunications Engineering Specialists
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of workers in the oil and gas sector, specialists in regions managing rapid 5G consumer expansion, and Chinese telecommunications organizations operating in the United States, operational focuses are diverging based on localized regulatory and industrial drivers [1][2][3]. In the oil and gas subsegment, the transition of private 5G from a discretionary tool to a business-critical utility alters the process of assessing existing facilities' needs [4] by prioritizing safety-critical connectivity over basic access [1]. This shift requires a more rigorous approach to estimating costs for system implementation [4] using total cost of ownership (TCO) models that incorporate workforce safety and operational reliability [1]. In regions experiencing massive consumer scale-up, the need to review and evaluate requests for system modifications [4] increases to manage network capacity as user bases scale [2]. This volume of growth increases the frequency of coordinating installation of new hardware [4] to maintain signal density across diverse geographies [2]. For Chinese telecommunications organizations facing regulatory crackdowns in the US, the role shifts toward implementing system renovation projects [4] specifically for the purpose of migrating or decommissioning data center infrastructure and network assets [3]. Inspecting sites to determine physical configuration [4] remains unlikely to change because physical conduit pathways and tower placements are constrained by existing urban and industrial footprints.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, specialists in these specific subsegments and regions will treat 5G infrastructure as a core utility or a regulatory liability, requiring higher reliability standards or managed decommissioning.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For these same subsegments and organizations, if current trajectories hold, the increased reliance on 5G for safety and mass-scale connectivity may lead to more stringent requirements for developing telecommunications disaster recovery plans [4] [1][2]. Because the network serves as a strategic backbone in industrial settings, the implementation of backup or recovery procedures [4] must evolve to support near-zero latency for safety-critical data [1]. In high-growth consumer regions, the requirement to monitor and analyze system performance [4] may shift toward the management of automated, AI-driven traffic steering to handle billion-user loads [2]. For organizations undergoing regulatory-driven exits, the focus may shift to documenting procedures for hardware and software installation and use [4] as part of permanent asset handover or site closures [3]. However, the need to consult with users, administrators, and engineers to identify technical requirements [4] will persist, as business and safety protocols remain grounded in human-defined operational constraints.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the role for these subsets will shift toward ensuring the disaster resilience and automated performance of high-density networks or the structured decommissioning of regulated assets.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For specialists in these specific industrial, regional, and organizational contexts, the long-term trajectory remains uncertain regarding whether 5G will be superseded by satellite-native integrated networks or 6G standards. One plausible outcome is that the role shifts toward the orchestration of virtualized network functions, reducing the time spent providing user support for diagnosing network and device problems [4]. A rival outcome is that the role becomes centered on extreme hardware specialization, where supervising maintenance of telecommunications equipment [4] dominates the workload due to the physical degradation of ruggedized hardware in harsh industrial environments [1]. The requirement to document technical specifications and operating standards [4] will likely resist change, as the high error cost in mission-critical sectors necessitates permanent, human-auditable records for regulatory compliance. It remains unknown if regulatory barriers between global telecom powers will permanently fragment the technical standards these specialists must implement.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, these specialists may transition into network orchestrators focusing on the health of virtualized, autonomous systems.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the role may converge on high-intensity physical maintenance of ruggedized infrastructure in industrial settings.*

title: Database Administrators
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For database administrators broadly, the adoption of AI-powered predictive tools for storage provisioning may alter how they identify, evaluate and recommend hardware or software technologies to achieve desired database performance [1]. Because these tools target "fear-driven over-provisioning" by predicting actual capacity needs, the manual estimation component of creating production databases and monitoring database performance may decrease in frequency [1], [2]. This shift moves the practitioner from heuristic-based capacity planning to the oversight of algorithmic predictions [1]. However, the implementation of security measures to safeguard information against unauthorized disclosure is unlikely to change in this period, as these tasks depend on specific organizational risk tolerances and regulatory mandates rather than storage optimization [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, database administrators may shift a portion of their capacity planning tasks from manual forecasting to the management of predictive AI tools.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For database administrators broadly, if current trajectories in predictive provisioning hold, the task of selecting and entering codes to monitor database performance could move toward an auditing role [1], [2]. Practitioners may spend less time on routine hardware recommendation and more time validating the accuracy of AI-driven allocation models to prevent under-provisioning during peak loads [1]. The necessity to correct errors and make necessary modifications to databases persists, as these tasks often involve resolving complex logical conflicts that predictive storage tools cannot address [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the role may evolve from active capacity provisioning to the auditing and validation of automated performance-tuning systems.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For database administrators broadly, the long-term trajectory suggests two rival outcomes based on the evolution of database architecture. In one scenario, the abstraction of the storage layer via AI could render the task of recommending hardware technologies obsolete, shifting the occupation toward high-level data governance and the development of standards for software acquisition [2]. In a competing scenario, the increasing complexity of hyper-scale environments may create a niche for specialists who manually override AI to manage extreme performance edge-cases [1]. It remains unknown whether future database management systems will fully decouple logical data modeling from physical resource allocation. The fundamental need to train users and answer questions about data access is likely to resist change, as it remains tied to human organizational hierarchies [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may transition into a governance-focused role as routine performance and capacity tasks become fully automated.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may bifurcate, with a small class of high-specialization engineers managing the physical constraints that AI cannot optimize.*

title: Database Architects
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of database architects operating in AI-integrated environments, including industrial and healthcare settings, the requirement to move AI from pilot phases to production now depends on the robustness of the underlying data architecture [4]. To support hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), these architects may alter how they develop data models for applications by integrating vector stores with traditional indices to enable semantic search [1]. The process of developing database architectural strategies may shift to prioritize governed data access for autonomous AI agents over traditional human-facing interfaces [2]. In industrial contexts, architects may focus on developing methods for integrating different products to unify fragmented operational data for real-time visibility [3]. However, the task of creating and enforcing database development standards for primary systems of record is unlikely to change, as the high error cost of data corruption in core financial or legal databases precludes the use of probabilistic storage [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, a subset of database architects will prioritize the design of hybrid architectures and governed access layers to transition AI agents and industrial intelligence from experimental pilots to operational production.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the same subset of workers in AI-integrated or industrial environments, if the adoption of agentic data access continues, the process of writing and coding logical and physical database descriptions may become partially automated through assistants that map natural language requests to schema elements [1][2]. Extrapolating from hybrid RAG trajectories, the focus of refining system performance and functionality may shift toward managing the synchronization between embedding models and source data to prevent semantic drift [1]. This may reduce the manual effort required for documenting database schemas as orchestration layers manage the relationship between raw data and its semantic representation [2]. Despite these changes, the task of identifying and evaluating industry trends to advise management will persist, as the selection of infrastructure involves strategic trade-offs and cost constraints that remain human-led.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, database design for this subsegment may shift toward automated schema mapping and the management of semantic synchronization, reducing the burden of manual documentation.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For the subset of architects managing AI-retrieval and industrial data systems, the long-term trajectory suggests a tension between autonomous optimization and regulatory requirements. If AI agents can dynamically execute the task of developing database architectural strategies based on real-time usage patterns, the human role in defining static physical descriptions may diminish [3]. Conversely, a rival outcome exists where new data provenance laws make the requirement to document and communicate database schemas more rigorous to ensure the auditability of AI-generated outputs. It remains unknown whether vector-based retrieval will eventually subsume all traditional indexing or if a permanent hybrid state will persist. The fundamental need to test databases and correct errors will resist change because the cost of systemic data failure remains catastrophic.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, database architecture for this subsegment may move toward a dynamic model where schemas are autonomously optimized by AI based on real-time usage patterns.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the role may shift toward high-rigor auditing and documentation of schemas to satisfy legal provenance requirements for AI systems.*

title: Data Warehousing Specialists
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For data warehousing specialists broadly, the adoption of AI-powered predictive tools may alter how they balance optimization of data access with resource utilization factors [9]. These tools use predictive analysis to align storage budgets with actual usage patterns, which may reduce the reliance on manual over-provisioning [1]. For a subset of workers in industrial settings, the need to unify fragmented operational data into single optimized foundations [2] may alter the way they develop data extraction procedures [4] and design warehouse database structures [5]. For a subset of workers in organizations deploying AI agents, the requirement to remove data access bottlenecks may shift the execution of creating metadata processes and frameworks [12] to ensure data is governed for autonomous agent consumption [3]. Mapping data between source systems and data warehouses [3] is unlikely to change in this period, as this task requires deep semantic understanding of legacy business logic and source-system idiosyncrasies that predictive tools do not address.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, data warehousing specialists may integrate AI tools for storage forecasting and industrial data unification, while a subset may specialize in optimizing warehouse structures and metadata for AI agent accessibility.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For data warehousing specialists broadly, if current trajectories in predictive storage [1] and industrial data optimization [2] hold, the focus of resource management may shift from manual tuning to the governance of autonomous scaling policies. Extrapolating from these trends, specialists could spend less time on the technical configuration of storage volumes and more on defining the operational constraints under which AI manages those volumes. For those focusing on AI agent support, the role may shift toward the continuous governance of "agent-ready" data pipelines to maintain the cleanliness required for autonomous agents [3]. In industrial contexts, the task of implementing business rules via stored procedures or middleware [16] may be increasingly driven by the requirements of real-time visibility foundations [4]. The task of verifying the structure, accuracy, or quality of warehouse data [2] is likely to remain a core human responsibility due to the high error costs associated with corporate financial and regulatory reporting.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may transition from manual resource tuning toward the governance of automated storage orchestration and the maintenance of specialized data environments optimized for AI agents.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For data warehousing specialists broadly, the long-term trajectory suggests two rival outcomes regarding the nature of the warehouse itself. In one scenario, the move toward predictive resource management [1], industrial unification [4], and agent-centric access [3] could lead to the emergence of "liquid" data architectures where static database structures are replaced by AI-managed ephemeral environments. In a competing scenario, strict regulatory requirements for data provenance and auditability could freeze the reliance on manually defined, transparent warehouse structures to ensure legal compliance. It remains unknown whether future compute-storage separation technologies will render the concept of "warehousing" as a distinct architectural pattern obsolete. The necessity of maintaining standards for nomenclature and organization [6] will likely resist change, as shared definitions remain the fundamental requirement for cross-organizational data utility.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may evolve into the governance of dynamic, AI-managed data environments that synthesize structures on demand.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may center on the rigorous maintenance of static, human-readable architectures to satisfy permanent regulatory audit requirements.*

title: Network and Computer Systems Administrators
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For network and computer systems administrators broadly, the integration of AI-driven storage analytics may reduce data over-provisioning as it alters how they analyze network and server resource consumption [5]. For administrators managing AI-integrated environments, the task to perform data backups and disaster recovery operations now extends to monitoring AI agent states and executing rollbacks of rogue agent actions [9]. For a subset of workers in organizations using cloud-native environments or enterprise Linux, the deployment of frontier agents may automate routine security testing and cloud operations within the task to maintain and administer computer networks [1][2]. In organizations using specific cloud project management tools, the task to analyze network and server resource consumption now includes the granular attribution of AI inference costs [4]. For administrators in enterprise mobile settings, the task to configure, monitor, and maintain email applications involves the technical implementation of end-to-end encryption for mobile devices [7]. In high-performance data center settings, the adoption of hardware optimizations to increase performance with fewer assets shifts the task to monitor network performance toward the oversight of denser resource concentrations [3]. In containerized or unpatched server environments, the task to diagnose, troubleshoot, and resolve hardware, software, or other network and system problems includes remediating authorization bypasses in Docker [6] and remote code execution flaws in server fleets [8]. The task to replace defective components remains unchanged because software agents lack the physical embodiment required for hardware swaps [2][3][5].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, administrators broadly may adopt predictive storage and agent-recovery tools, while those in cloud, Linux, and enterprise mobile subsegments integrate autonomous agents for routine maintenance and the deployment of enhanced encryption.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For administrators in these broad and subsegment contexts, if current trajectories hold, the task to diagnose, troubleshoot, and resolve network problems may shift toward the auditing of agent-generated diagnostics and the management of agent-state recovery [2][9]. Extrapolating from predictive storage trends, the task to analyze network and server resource consumption could move toward a model of continuous, autonomous capacity rightsizing [5]. The task to confer with network users about solutions to existing system problems is likely to persist unchanged because these interactions require organizational and social context not present in technical logs [2][5]. High-level security policy definition within the task to plan, coordinate, and implement network security measures remains a human-led function due to the liability associated with infrastructure-wide access controls [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, workflow integration for these subsegments could deepen, shifting the administrator's role toward auditing AI-generated diagnostics and capacity optimizations.*

## Far (2046–2051)

Within these technology-driven environments, the evolution of the role depends on whether regulatory regimes grant autonomous agents the authority to execute structural changes in critical infrastructure. A primary unknown is the legal threshold for liability when an agent-led modification causes a catastrophic network outage. The task to design, configure, and test computer hardware and networking software resists full automation due to the high error cost of structural architectural failures [2][9]. Rival outcomes depend on whether the need for "rollback" capabilities for autonomous agents [9] suggests an inherent instability that mandates permanent human oversight.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may transition into a supervisory role focused on liability management and the validation of agent-driven architectural shifts.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, persistent risks in autonomous infrastructure management may restrict agent authority to non-critical tasks, preserving the administrator's role as the primary executor of all structural network changes.*

title: Computer Programmers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For this occupation broadly, the integration of terminal-based AI agents alters the task of writing, analyzing, reviewing, and rewriting programs by shifting the workflow from manual code entry to agent-led generation [1][4][7]. Multi-model verification features, such as cross-model review, modify the mechanism for correcting errors by providing automated second opinions to validate logical consistency [5]. For a subset of workers in logistics, the use of specialized agents may automate the maintenance of computer programs that handle specific jobs, such as managing rate complexity [2]. In organizations adopting AI-driven development platforms, these tools scale the ability to write and update programs across enterprise infrastructures [6]. For entry-level programmers, the automation of basic authorship tasks may reduce the demand for those performing routine coding, potentially narrowing the traditional career entry point [3]. However, the emergence of "vibe coding"—where developers rely on high-level prompts without manual verification—introduces risks that complicate the task of correcting errors when AI-generated logic fails silently [8]. The task of consulting with managerial, engineering, and technical personnel to clarify program intent is unlikely to change, as agent-led generation still requires high-fidelity human specifications to avoid logical drift [2][5].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, computer programmers may transition from manual code authorship to the supervision of terminal-based agents, while the entry point for junior-level roles may narrow.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For this occupation broadly, if the cost of proprietary agents is offset by open-source alternatives [1], autonomous agents may become the primary mechanism for correcting errors and rechecking programs through iterative, self-correcting loops [5]. Extrapolating from specialized deployments in logistics [2] and the automation of routine scripts [9], the translation of complex business logic into executable code could reduce the manual effort required for the revision, repair, or expansion of existing programs [6]. The requirement to compile and write documentation of program development will likely persist as a human-led activity to ensure system auditability in regulated environments [5]. The task of investigating whether networks, workstations, or peripheral equipment are responding to program instructions is unlikely to change, as symbolic agents lack the physical observability required for hardware-level troubleshooting.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may shift toward the validation and orchestration of AI-generated logic, with routine maintenance becoming an automated process across various organizational settings.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For this occupation broadly, the long-term trajectory depends on whether AI-generated code remains legible to human overseers. One plausible outcome is that the task of preparing detailed workflow charts and diagrams is fully replaced by the management of autonomous agents that handle the entire lifecycle of maintaining computer programs [1][4]. A competing outcome is that the accumulation of opaque, AI-generated legacy code creates a "complexity trap," where the loss of human-authored mental models forces a return to manual revision and repair of systems that agents cannot safely modify without introducing regressions [3][8]. It remains unknown whether professional liability regimes will mandate a human author of record for all production code, which would constrain the degree of agent autonomy. The application of symbolic logic to resolve deep structural contradictions in software architecture is likely to resist full automation even at this horizon.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the role may evolve into a high-level system orchestrator, where the programmer manages a fleet of autonomous agents handling the full software lifecycle.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the accumulation of unmanageable AI-generated legacy code may force a resurgence in manual programming to recover system stability and transparency.*

title: Software Developers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For software developers broadly, and specifically those in AI infrastructure, XR prototyping, and open-source maintenance, the task of develop or direct software system testing or validation procedures is being modified by cross-model review features to automate the validation of AI-generated plans [17] and LLM-driven mutation testing to improve compliance [3]. For developers broadly, the task of modify existing software incorporates agentic tools to automate environment management [9] and the automation of scheduled tasks through built-in AI routines [41], though these are constrained by privacy risks regarding the volume of system information captured by cloud-based agents [5]. In the XR subsegment, the task of design, develop and modify software systems shifts toward intent-based prototyping using AI-driven blocks [2], while for specialists in AI infrastructure, the same task emphasizes the development of specialized communication libraries for GPU optimization [8] and the implementation of distributed parallelism for LLM inference [20][42]. For developers implementing on-device AI, the task of design, develop and modify software systems is shifting toward local model execution and hardware acceleration [19]. A shift toward "vibe coding"—prompting AI to generate code without deep understanding of underlying logic—is introducing higher levels of technical debt into the task of design, develop and modify software systems [39]. Open-source maintainers tasked to supervise the work of programmers face increased overhead due to high volumes of low-quality AI-generated contributions [13] and industrialized social engineering attacks targeting the software supply chain [6][11][16][21][38], while the IDE has emerged as a targeted infection vector for stealthy malware [36]. For developers performing security reviews, the task of modify existing software now requires manual verification of Git commit identities to prevent AI reviewers from being fooled by identity spoofing [46]. In organizations using enterprise agent registries, the task of analyze information to determine, recommend, and plan installation of a new system shifts from custom creation toward the discovery and reuse of existing agents [29][32] and the management of model transitions to avoid application failure during deprecations [28]. The task of analyze user needs and software requirements is unlikely to change because current tools cannot independently evaluate the feasibility of designs against volatile real-world time and cost constraints [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, autonomous agents become standard for routine drafting and environment management, while an increased security burden on the open-source supply chain and local IDEs raises the cost of maintainership.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the cohorts described in the near term, if current trajectories hold, the availability of low-cost or free open-source agentic alternatives may expand the use of autonomous agents for the task of design, develop and modify software systems into organizations previously constrained by proprietary tool pricing [1]. Extrapolating from prototyping trends, intent-based specification in the XR subsegment may become the primary method for initial development, though manual syntax persists for implementing complex, non-standard logic [2]. For developers in security-critical subsegments, the task of develop or direct software system testing or validation procedures may shift toward defensive auditing of AI-led remediations following failures in automated bug-bounty workflows [25]. For entry-level developers in academic settings, the task of design, develop and modify software systems may be reduced to higher-level orchestration as basic implementation is automated [4]. The task of confer with systems analysts, engineers, programmers and others is unlikely to change because the coordination of conflicting stakeholder requirements across different organizational silos remains a human-centric negotiation process.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the role of the entry-level developer shifts toward agent orchestration and auditing, while high-level system design remains the primary human-led activity.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For software developers in the settings identified in the near term, the sustainability of the occupation depends on whether the technical debt accumulated through "vibe coding" [39] triggers a systemic failure in codebase maintainability. One rival outcome suggests a transition where humans exclusively perform the task of analyze user needs and software requirements, while the entire pipeline of design, develop and modify software systems is handled by agentic swarms. Another rival outcome involves a retrenchment toward manual, verified "hard-coding" for critical infrastructure to mitigate the risks of industrialized supply chain attacks [6][16]. It remains unknown if AI can develop a mechanistic understanding of "correctness" that does not rely on probabilistic imitation of existing (and potentially flawed) code. The task of coordinate installation of software system in air-gapped or high-security environments is likely to resist change due to the absolute requirement for physical human presence and manual verification.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, software development evolves into a purely architectural role, with the implementation and validation tasks fully delegated to autonomous agentic systems.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, a "verification crisis" forces a return to manual coding and rigorous human-led audits for all non-trivial systems to ensure security and stability.*

title: Software Quality Assurance Analysts and Testers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For software quality assurance analysts and testers broadly, large language models may automate mutation testing and the verification of compliance adherence [1], reducing the manual effort required to develop testing programs [1]. AI-led discovery of complex vulnerabilities may shift the task of identifying, analyzing, and documenting problems with program function toward the validation of high-complexity AI-detected flaws [9]. Conversely, the proliferation of low-quality AI-generated code may increase the manual workload associated with identifying, analyzing, and documenting problems with program function [3]. For a subset of workers in rapid-application-development environments, a surge in low-rigor "vibe coding" submissions may increase the burden of identifying program deviance from standards [6]. For a subset of workers in AI platform development, the emergence of "silent failures"—where system health indicators remain positive despite functional output degradation—necessitates new methods to monitor program performance [7]. In the autonomous vehicle subsegment, operational failures in diverse environments [2][8] indicate a requirement for more rigorous edge-case validation when designing test plans, scenarios, scripts, or procedures [2][8]. For workers in generative AI applications, the high rate of factual errors in outputs increases the burden of identifying problems with content [4], while some organizations may replace manual scenario scripting with high-fidelity AI user simulators to identify edge cases [10]. In regulated industries using generative AI, the task of documenting test procedures and specifying standards for release readiness may shift from probabilistic sampling to formal verification using automated reasoning [12]. The task of investigating customer problems referred by technical support is unlikely to change in this horizon because it requires interpreting unstructured, environment-specific user reports that lack standardized error logs [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the occupation may see a divergence where automation handles mutation testing and deep vulnerability discovery, while analysts face an increased volume of verification work to filter AI-generated code and validate non-deterministic outputs.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For testers in high-complexity and safety-critical environments: if current trajectories hold, the task of updating automated test scripts to ensure currency may shift toward managing dynamic, model-generated updates informed by AI performance predictions [11]. Extrapolating from failures in autonomous deployments [2][8] and the development of ethics frameworks for autonomous systems, the task of designing test plans in the autonomous subsegment may transition toward the orchestration of simulation-based edge-case libraries and fairness-audit protocols [5][8]. If AI-generated code continues to introduce subtle, plausible errors and AI-led detection tools become prevalent, the core analyst role may shift from initial bug discovery to a triage-heavy function of verifying plausible AI claims [3][9]. Participating in product design reviews to provide input on functional requirements will likely persist unchanged because it depends on human negotiation of schedules and stakeholder priorities [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the analyst's role in high-complexity environments may transition toward the orchestration of automated simulations and the high-volume triage of AI-generated defect reports.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For testers in high-reliability and large-scale engineering settings: one plausible outcome is that LLMs and automated reasoning automate the validation of compliance-heavy test suites, reducing the analyst's role to auditing LLM-generated evidence [1][12]. A rival outcome is that the non-deterministic nature of AI systems creates an infinite state space that resists full automation, requiring analysts to shift toward adversarial probing and systemic fragility analysis [7]. It remains unknown whether formal verification can scale to the entirety of evolving, interconnected software ecosystems. Final sign-off on product release readiness is likely to resist change due to the legal and liability constraints associated with certifying safety-critical software [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the role may evolve into a high-level compliance auditor who validates the formal proofs generated by automated reasoning systems.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the role may shift toward an adversarial specialist focused on identifying systemic failure modes that automated tools cannot predict.*

title: Web Developers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For web developers broadly, the integration of terminal-based autonomous agents into development environments may alter the task of writing supporting code by allowing the generation, debugging, and deployment of code to occur directly within the command-line interface [1][2][8]. Because cross-model review features are emerging in CLI tools, the task of evaluating code to ensure it is properly structured may shift from manual line-by-line inspection toward auditing automated second opinions provided by competing models [5]. For a subset of workers managing content-heavy sites, the adoption of AI-powered CMS platforms may shift the task of designing, building, or maintaining web sites toward managing automated structural deployments [3]. The task of incorporating technical considerations into web site design plans may increasingly prioritize machine-readability and specific metadata structures to ensure visibility for AI search agents [4]. Furthermore, the task of writing supporting code for web applications now includes integrating live AI browser agents directly into frontend frameworks like React [6]. While AI-accelerated generation reduces build time, the task of evaluating code to ensure it meets industry standards must now specifically include verifying that automated tools have not ignored accessibility requirements [7]. Analyzing user needs to determine technical requirements is unlikely to change yet because this task requires the interpersonal negotiation of ambiguous business goals and stakeholder constraints [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, web developers may increasingly rely on terminal-integrated agents for code drafting and shift their focus toward auditing agent outputs, managing AI-native CMS deployments, and optimizing site structures for AI search discovery.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For web developers broadly, if the availability of low-cost or open-source autonomous agents scales to offset the high subscription costs of proprietary tools [1][8], the task of selecting programming languages or design tools may shift toward agent-led optimization based on real-time target environment constraints. Extrapolating from current cross-model review capabilities, the manual effort required to perform web site tests could decrease as agents autonomously cycle through planning, implementation, and verification [5]. For workers in the CMS subsegment, the continued adoption of AI-native platforms may further reduce the necessity for manual evaluation or recommendation of server hardware or software by abstracting infrastructure management [3]. The requirement to confer with management or development teams to prioritize needs persists because these tasks involve organizational politics and subjective value judgments that resist algorithmic resolution [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may transition toward the orchestration of autonomous agent pipelines for code generation and verification, provided the cost of deployment remains low.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For web developers broadly, the long-term trajectory depends on whether the structural model of web application databases and interactive interfaces remains stable [2]. One plausible outcome involves the high-degree automation of writing supporting code, shifting the developer's primary role toward high-level systems architecture and security auditing [1]. A rival outcome exists if the proliferation of agent-generated code introduces systemic fragility, creating a requirement for deep-stack manual expertise to resolve critical infrastructure failures that agents cannot diagnose. Documenting technical factors such as server load and bandwidth resists change because these tasks are grounded in physical hardware constraints and energy limits [2]. It remains unknown whether the conceptual distinction between a web developer and a software developer will persist as toolchains converge.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may evolve into a specialized auditing and architectural role focusing on the governance of autonomous generation pipelines.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may see a resurgence in demand for manual, deep-stack coding expertise to remediate systemic instabilities caused by legacy AI-generated code.*

title: Web and Digital Interface Designers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For the occupation broadly, the acceleration of AI-driven site generation may increase the requirement for rapid auditing to incorporate technical considerations into Web site design plans, specifically regarding accessibility standards [4]. Simultaneously, the emergence of AI agents as intermediaries between customers and businesses may reduce the reliance on designing visual funnels to develop Web site maps and page templates [13] optimized for human browsing [2]. For a subset of workers in extended reality (XR) contexts, tools combining large language models with XR blocks may accelerate the ability to create Web models or prototypes [7] [1]. For designers of child-facing interfaces, the adoption of safety frameworks may introduce new constraints when incorporating technical considerations regarding age-appropriate safeguards [19] [3]. For a subset of designers using agentic design platforms, natural language prompts may shift the process of developing new visual design concepts [10] toward conversation-based iteration of editable layouts [5]. It is unlikely that the need to conduct user research to determine design requirements [4] will diminish, as human intent must still be validated even if the final interaction is agent-mediated [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the occupation broadly may shift toward rapid accessibility auditing and agent-readable structures, while subsegments in XR and child-safety design experience accelerated prototyping and new regulatory constraints respectively.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the occupation broadly, if current trajectories toward agent-mediated commerce hold, the task of designing, building, or maintaining Web sites [8] may pivot from visual interface creation to the design of structured data environments optimized for agent navigation [2]. This shift would prioritize machine-readability over aesthetic conversion funnels for standard B2C transactions. However, the development and documentation of style guidelines for Web site content [9] will likely persist for high-value brand interactions where direct human sensory experience remains a competitive differentiator. Extrapolating from current prototyping trends, the role for those in immersive segments may shift toward orchestrating interaction logic rather than static layout [1].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, interface design for a broad segment of e-commerce may shift toward agent-centric architectures, reducing the relative importance of visual layout optimization.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For the occupation broadly, the long-term state depends on whether users fully delegate digital interactions to agents or whether a preference for sensory, visual browsing persists [2]. One plausible outcome involves the transition of the designer's role into an architect of non-visual interaction protocols for autonomous agents. A rival outcome suggests that accelerated spatial prototyping tools [1] could drive a resurgence in highly complex, immersive human interfaces as a premium alternative to agent-driven automation. A critical unknown remains the rate of hardware adoption for immersive interfaces relative to the speed of agent-based automation. Even at this horizon, the necessity of ensuring functionality against accessibility standards [19] is expected to resist full automation due to the persistent variability of human cognitive and physical needs.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation broadly may evolve into the design of non-visual, agent-to-agent interaction protocols.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation broadly may pivot toward high-sensory, immersive human interfaces as a premium alternative to agent-driven automation.*

title: Video Game Designers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of designers in small studios seeking funding and organizations facing corporate disputes, alongside the broader occupation's adoption of AI asset tools: designers in conflict-facing organizations may modify how they create core game features, including storylines and character biographies, by integrating real-world business litigation into downloadable content [1]. For designers in smaller studios, the use of dedicated matchmaking platforms may alter how they present new game design concepts to potential publishers to reduce discovery fatigue [3]. Across the occupation, the adoption of photo-to-volume AI may streamline preparing three-dimensional mock-ups and initial game sketches [2]. However, the task of balancing and adjusting gameplay experiences to ensure commercial success is unlikely to change, as it relies on iterative human playtesting rather than asset generation or narrative delivery [2]. The fundamental requirement to document all aspects of formal game design remains a stable constraint for technical production [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, designers in specific organizational contexts may use narrative DLC for corporate communication and matchmaking platforms for publisher discovery, while the broader occupation adopts AI for 3D asset prototyping.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the same subsegments and organizational contexts: if matchmaking platforms become the primary channel for discovery, the process of presenting new game design concepts may shift toward standardized, data-driven portfolios to meet publisher criteria [3]. Extrapolating from the adoption of volume-generation tools, designers may reduce the time spent preparing two-dimensional concept layouts in favor of rapid 3D prototyping [2]. The use of narrative DLC for corporate commentary may remain a niche practice, contingent on the commercial viability of such meta-narratives [1]. Regular design reviews likely persist unchanged because these evaluations focus on experiential quality which AI-generated assets do not inherently solve [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the presentation of design concepts may become more standardized for publishers, while AI-driven 3D prototyping reduces the reliance on 2D concept layouts.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For the same subsets of designers: rival outcomes exist regarding the integration of corporate litigation into game narratives, depending on whether legal frameworks normalize in-game commentary or treat it as a liability [1]. It remains unknown whether photo-to-volume AI will eventually automate the creation of character biographies and role-play mechanics, or if these remain strictly human-driven tasks [2]. One uncertainty is whether matchmaking platforms will evolve into automated curation systems that bypass the need for designers to present concepts to humans entirely [3]. The task of devising missions, challenges, or puzzles resists change at this horizon because it requires a deep understanding of player psychology and frustration thresholds [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, narrative DLC becomes a recognized medium for corporate litigation for a subset of designers facing public scrutiny.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, legal risks associated with in-game corporate commentary lead to a systemic rejection of the practice, restricting it to fringe cases.*

title: Web Administrators
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of web administrators managing WordPress-based environments or content-heavy publishing sites, technical priorities are bifurcating between automation and defensive hardening. In organizations adopting AI-integrated CMS platforms, the use of sandboxed plugins and serverless scaling may reduce the need to manually implement updates, upgrades, and patches [1] or configure server hardware to manage traffic spikes [1]. Simultaneously, for administrators in publishing settings, the emergence of third-party AI scrapers [2] necessitates the implementation of specific web site security measures [8] and more frequent monitoring for unauthorized scraping patterns [1]. The use of passkey authentication alters the mechanism used to implement security measures [1]. Despite these shifts, the need to collaborate with development teams to resolve usability issues [9] is unlikely to change because usability requires qualitative human judgment of user experience.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, administrators within these subsegments will see a reduction in routine server maintenance tasks offset by an increased requirement to deploy technical countermeasures against AI-driven content scraping.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For these same subsegments of administrators, if current trajectories hold, the role may shift from operational execution to environment and access governance. Extrapolating from the move toward serverless architectures, the task of installing or configuring web server software [17] may become a negligible part of the workflow for those using AI-powered CMS tools [1]. If the AI content licensing market continues to grow [2], the task of implementing security measures [8] may shift toward managing granular, identity-based access and licensing rules [5]. Administrators may spend more time on these higher-level functions, which are governed by organizational policy rather than technical constraints. The core need to document application and web site changes [12] persists because audit trails remain a requirement for institutional accountability.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the technical administration of these environments will shift toward the governance of AI-managed configurations and the enforcement of content-access protocols.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For administrators in these specific subsets, the long-term trajectory depends on the resolution of the conflict between content publishers and AI aggregators. One outcome involves the adoption of standardized, automated licensing protocols that eliminate the need for manual blocking, shifting the role toward a purely policy-driven compliance function. A rival outcome is that adversarial AI scrapers evolve to create opaque, systemic server failures, increasing the demand for deep forensic skills to determine sources of web page or server problems [6]. It remains unknown whether decentralized web protocols will replace the centralized CMS model entirely. However, the necessity to test backup or recovery plans regularly [14] will likely resist automation due to the catastrophic cost of total data loss.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the role for this subsegment may evolve into a compliance-focused function as content access and server environments become fully abstracted and automated.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the role may shift toward high-complexity forensic troubleshooting to resolve systemic failures caused by sophisticated, autonomous AI-driven scraping and attack vectors.*

title: Geographic Information Systems Technologists and Technicians
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For GIS technologists operating in regions with national 3D city-modeling initiatives, such as Japan, the workflow for geospatial data acquisition is shifting from manual generation to the integration of open-access digital twins [1]. This shift reduces the reliance on manual digitizing of maps or keyboard entry of tabular data [2]. Instead, these workers primarily collect, compile, or integrate GIS data [2] by importing existing high-fidelity 3D models into local databases [1]. Because these open-access models provide a standardized baseline, the task of producing data layers [2] becomes an exercise in filtering and layering existing data rather than original creation. Technical support to users regarding the operation of GIS databases [2] remains unlikely to change significantly, as the complexity of software configuration and client-specific requirements still necessitates human mediation.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, for technologists in contexts adopting open-access city models, the role shifts from primary data creation toward the integration and management of standardized 3D geospatial datasets.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For technologists in these same urban-modeling contexts, if the adoption of open-access digital twins continues, the focus of maintaining or modifying existing GIS databases [2] may shift toward synchronization and version control [1]. The mechanism driving this is the transition from static map layers to dynamic models that require frequent updates to reflect physical urban changes. As the volume of open-access 3D data increases, the task of reviewing incoming data for currency and accuracy [2] will likely persist, as the reliability of government-provided models must be validated against local site-specific observations. The need to confer with users to troubleshoot applications [2] remains unchanged due to the inherent variability in how different organizations implement these 3D models.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, for technologists in regions with mature digital twin infrastructures, the primary technical challenge shifts from data acquisition to the curation and validation of high-frequency model updates.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For technologists in regions utilizing these digital twins, the long-term trajectory depends on the resolution of the tension between open-access standards and proprietary urban data silos. If open-access models become the universal substrate, the task of designing integrated GIS spatial databases [2] may evolve into managing real-time data streams that automatically update the 3D environment. However, a rival outcome exists where proprietary constraints limit the utility of open models, forcing technologists to continue performing manual conversion of other sources of digital data [2] to bridge incompatible systems. It remains unknown whether real-time sensor integration will eventually eliminate the need for manual data review. Meeting with clients to discuss technical specifications [2] will likely resist change, as the conceptual goals of urban planning remain human-directed.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, for technologists in open-data regions, the role evolves into the management of automated, real-time synchronization between physical cities and their digital twins.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, persistent data fragmentation forces technologists to remain specialized in the manual translation and conversion of incompatible proprietary spatial datasets.*

title: Document Management Specialists
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For document management specialists broadly, the adoption of digital annotation systems may alter the administration of revision control and secure document workflows [2]. Because these systems replace paper markups with real-time collaborative digital layers, specialists may shift how they administer document and system access rights and revision control to accommodate concurrent edits while maintaining the integrity of master documents [2]. For a subset of workers in manufacturing environments, the use of AI translation technology may alter how they prepare and record changes to official documents [1]. In these settings, the mechanism of automated translation allows for faster synchronization of compliance records across multilingual workforces, potentially reducing the manual overhead of managing regional document variants [1]. However, conducting needs assessments to identify document management requirements is unlikely to change in the near term because these assessments depend on the specific physical and organizational constraints of the end user's environment [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the occupation may see a shift toward managing dynamic digital annotation workflows broadly, while manufacturing subsegments may partially automate the versioning of multilingual compliance documents.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For document management specialists broadly, if current trajectories hold, the task of implementing electronic document processing, retrieval, and distribution systems may shift toward the management of "living" documents that incorporate permanent digital annotation histories [2]. The mechanism driving this is the transition from static versioning to continuous, trackable digital collaboration [2]. For the subset of workers in manufacturing, extrapolating from current AI translation trends, the task of monitoring regulatory activity may shift toward the auditing of automated translation pipelines to ensure technical and legal nuance is preserved [1]. Despite these shifts, documenting technical functions and specifications for content management systems will likely persist because the underlying system architectures remain proprietary and require human-authored documentation for audit and recovery purposes [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the role may transition from managing static records toward the oversight of continuous collaboration streams and automated translation audits.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For document management specialists, the future of the role may diverge based on the evolution of digital provenance and regulatory mandates. One plausible outcome is that the development of content classification taxonomies becomes largely autonomous, shifting the specialist's role toward high-level policy governance of autonomous systems. A rival outcome is that the rise of sophisticated digital alterations necessitates a return to rigid, human-certified "gold standard" records, increasing the specialist's role as a legal custodian of authenticity. It remains unknown whether global standards for digital record-keeping will unify or fragment further. The requirement to implement procedures for the secure destruction of electronic records will likely resist change due to the persistent nature of legal liability and statutory retention mandates [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, specialists may shift primarily toward high-level system governance and the auditing of autonomous content lifecycles.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, specialists may evolve into specialized authenticity certifiers, where the primary value is the legal validation of document provenance.*

title: Penetration Testers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For penetration testers broadly, the deployment of frontier cybersecurity models alters the task to identify security system weaknesses by automating the discovery of zero-day vulnerabilities [14][15]. Because threat actors utilize AI-assisted vectors to target software supply chains and exploit Git identity spoofing to bypass AI-driven code reviews, testers must integrate these mechanisms when they develop infiltration tests that exploit device vulnerabilities [5][42]. The emergence of AI-specific attack surfaces—including AI injection [11], agentic memory attacks [32], and the exploitation of non-human identities [12]—requires testers to expand how they identify new threat tactics, techniques, or procedures [40]. In organizations using cloud-native infrastructure, frontier agents automate specific portions of the task to develop and execute tests that simulate the techniques of known cyber threat actors [1]. For a subsegment of workers in the automotive sector, automated V2G security testing streamlines the process of testing the security of systems within networked vehicle environments [33]. For a subset of independent security researchers, the task to identify security system weaknesses is being partially displaced by AI-led discovery, leading to the pausing of certain bug bounty programs [19]. The task to assess the physical security of servers, systems, or network devices remains unlikely to change because it requires manual on-site hardware verification [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, penetration testers will integrate autonomous vulnerability discovery and AI-specific attack vectors into their workflows, while specialists in cloud and automotive sectors adopt domain-specific agents for simulation.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For penetration testers broadly: if current trajectories in autonomous vulnerability mapping and discovery hold, the task to identify security system weaknesses may shift from manual discovery to the verification and auditing of AI-generated attack paths [10][18]. Extrapolating from trends in red team workflow automation, the task to gather cyber intelligence to identify vulnerabilities could be partially managed by orchestration platforms that standardize the reconnaissance process [3]. In heavily regulated financial environments, the role may shift toward validating the risk briefs provided by regulators regarding AI-driven cyber risks [28]. However, the task to write audit reports to communicate technical and procedural findings persists as a human-led activity because the attribution of risk and alignment with organizational business logic require human accountability [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, technical exploitation may shift toward the auditing of autonomous AI-led attack chains, while formal reporting and regulatory validation remain human-centric due to accountability constraints.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For penetration testers broadly: the long-term status of the task to test the security of systems depends on whether AI agents achieve a stable capacity to discover novel vulnerabilities without human-defined heuristics [4][10]. It remains unknown if the acceleration of AI-driven discovery will lead to real-time automated remediation that effectively closes the window for manual penetration testing [17]. The task to discuss security solutions with information technology teams or management resists change because negotiating risk appetite and organizational priorities requires human-centric social navigation [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, autonomous agents handle the majority of technical vulnerability discovery and exploitation, shifting the human role to strategic risk orchestration.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the role evolves into a specialized "adversarial auditor" position, focusing exclusively on the failure modes of the AI agents that manage both attack and defense.*

title: Information Security Engineers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For information security engineers broadly, the proliferation of residential proxies renders IP-based reputation systems insufficient, shifting the task of developing or installing software to protect sensitive information toward identity-centric verification and zero-trust architectures [5]. To identify security system weaknesses, engineers must implement kernel-level protections to counter "bring your own vulnerable driver" (BYOVD) techniques used by ransomware to disable endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools [6][36]. The prevalence of unmanaged non-human identities and API keys, which drive a majority of cloud breaches, alters the task of implementing solutions to information security problems by requiring the design of automated discovery and rotation systems for service accounts [14][43]. The emergence of agentic memory attacks and AI-injection vulnerabilities, such as GrafanaGhost, shifts the task of coordinating monitoring of networks toward auditing prompt-injection vectors and session-crossing data leaks [13][18][31]. For engineers in critical infrastructure settings, targeted attacks on PLC and SCADA systems shift the task of identifying security system weaknesses toward the hardening of operational technology [12][16][28]. The manual verification of physical hardware seals on air-gapped servers is unlikely to change, as these protocols rely on physical tamper-evidence rather than digital signals.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, information security engineers will transition from IP-based perimeter defenses toward identity-centric controls and kernel-level hardening, while implementing specialized lifecycle management for non-human identities.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For information security engineers broadly, if high-capability cybersecurity models such as Mythos and GPT-5.4-Cyber move from limited preview to operational deployment, the task of identifying security system weaknesses may shift from manual penetration tests toward overseeing automated vulnerability discovery and remediation loops [9][10][19][34][42]. Extrapolating from current agentic attack speeds, the task of coordinating monitoring of networks for security breaches may shift toward the orchestration of autonomous defense agents that anticipate attack vectors before they are deployed [11][15]. For a subset of workers managing high-sensitivity data, the emergence of quantum computing threats may shift the task of developing software to protect sensitive information toward the implementation of post-quantum cryptographic standards [26][41]. The requirement for human sign-off on high-impact policy changes, such as the total isolation of critical infrastructure segments during a suspected breach, persists because the catastrophic error cost of a security policy failure requires human accountability.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may shift from manual monitoring and testing toward the orchestration of autonomous predictive defense systems, provided that high-capability AI models are integrated into operational workflows.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For a subset of workers managing autonomous systems, the long-term trajectory may lead to the adoption of mission-scale zero-trust platforms to govern non-human identities and autonomous agents [24]. A primary uncertainty remains whether regulatory regimes will mandate human-in-the-loop overrides for all autonomous security actions or permit bounded autonomy for system-wide remediation. The fundamental logic of access control—the principle of least privilege—resists change even at this horizon, as it remains the primary mechanism for limiting blast radii in any networked environment.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, security engineering for autonomous systems is defined by the administration of zero-trust governance platforms that manage non-human identities with bounded autonomy.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, strict regulatory mandates for human-in-the-loop overrides prevent the adoption of autonomous remediation, maintaining the engineer's role as a primary manual decision-maker for system-wide security states.*

title: Digital Forensics Analysts
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For digital forensics analysts broadly, the rise of AI-generated synthetic media and deepfakes alters the requirements for performing file signature analysis to verify files on storage media [3][8]. The proliferation of synthetic media complicates the task to write reports, sign affidavits, or give depositions for legal proceedings, as analysts must now establish mechanistic provenance to distinguish fabrications from authentic data [3][8]. In organizations facing "ghost breaches," the task to write technical summaries to report findings now includes forensic verification to disprove incidents that are actually AI-generated narratives [12]. For analysts investigating network intrusions, the use of adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) attacks via router compromises shifts how they analyze log files toward the identification of hijacked session tokens rather than simple credential theft [5]. The use of registered LLCs and synthetic corporate identities by state-sponsored actors requires analysts to adjust how they develop plans for investigating alleged computer crimes to include multi-layered entity verification [2][7]. The introduction of domain-specific models such as GPT-5.4-Cyber may automate components of recovering data or decrypting seized data and the analysis of malware [13]. For a subset of workers investigating mobile-based banking fraud, the use of obfuscated VBS files and specialized Android trojans requires updated scripts to automate tasks, such as parsing large data files [1][6]. The task to adhere to legal policies and procedures related to handling digital media is unlikely to change because judicial chain-of-custody requirements remain structurally independent of the technical nature of the evidence [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, forensic verification workflows will integrate synthetic media detection and session-token telemetry as standard components of evidence validation.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For digital forensics analysts broadly, if current trajectories of synthetic identity proliferation and AI-driven fraud hold, the task to analyze log files to identify perpetrators may shift from detecting technical anomalies toward identifying longitudinal behavioral inconsistencies [2][3][7]. Extrapolating from the increase in AI-boosted online fraud losses, the process to conduct predictive or reactive analyses on security measures could move toward identifying systemic bot-network patterns rather than isolated actor signatures [4][9]. The requirement to write reports, sign affidavits, or give depositions for legal proceedings persists unchanged because the erosion of trust in digital records increases the necessity for human experts to attest to the provenance of evidence [3][8]. This shift is conditional on the development of telemetry capable of distinguishing biological behavioral patterns from high-fidelity synthetic simulations.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, attribution efforts will rely more on long-term behavioral baselining and less on isolated technical triggers to distinguish legitimate users from synthetic impersonators.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For digital forensics analysts broadly, the ability to provide definitive attribution remains uncertain due to the potential for high-fidelity simulation of authorized user behavior by advanced AI [3]. One plausible outcome involves the adoption of immutable, hardware-level provenance logging that reduces the reliance on post-incident log analysis. A rival outcome involves a systemic decline in the admissibility of purely digital evidence in court, shifting the analyst's role toward the verification of analog side-channels and physical artifacts. The task to preserve and maintain digital forensic evidence for analysis resists change because evidentiary integrity remains the fundamental prerequisite for legal admissibility regardless of the evidence's format.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation shifts toward the verification of hardware-attested provenance logs, reducing the prevalence of traditional post-incident reconstruction.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation pivots toward the analysis of physical and analog artifacts as digital evidence becomes too easily simulated to meet legal standards of proof.*

title: Blockchain Engineers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For the occupation broadly, research into quantum-safe algorithms may shift the evaluation criteria used to design and verify cryptographic protocols to protect private information [3]. For a subset of engineers managing public repositories, the prevalence of token giveaway scams may alter how they assess blockchain threats, specifically regarding unprotected keys [1]. In regulated financial settings, such as those testing sovereign stablecoins in Switzerland, there may be an increased focus on the task to design and deploy blockchain design patterns that ensure transaction immutability for pegged assets [2]. These institutional efforts may shift the focus toward integrating these assets into existing banking infrastructures [2]. The task of automating the deployment of software updates over geographically distributed network nodes is unlikely to change, as the orchestration of node updates is functionally independent of the cryptographic primitives being secured [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, blockchain engineering will be characterized by an experimental shift toward quantum-resistant cryptographic criteria alongside a divergence between high-caution open-source workflows and regulated financial sandbox deployments.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

If current trajectories hold, for the occupation broadly, the transition from research to operational deployment of quantum-safe security protocols may shift the core requirement to design and verify cryptographic protocols [3]. For engineers in regulated financial settings, extrapolating from current regional tests, the task of designing and developing blockchain technologies for finance may shift toward the creation of interoperable, quantum-resistant stablecoin standards [2][3]. For those in open-source environments, the need to assess blockchain threats will likely persist as social engineering attack vectors evolve [1]. The requirement to discuss data needs with engineers, product managers, or data scientists to identify blockchain requirements remains unchanged, as these coordination tasks are driven by organizational needs rather than technological shifts [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may bifurcate into a specialized class of financial infrastructure architects focused on stablecoin interoperability and a defensive class of security engineers focused on maintaining quantum-resistant public networks.*

## Far (2046–2051)

Scope remains limited to the broader occupation and the specific financial and open-source settings established in the near term. Rival outcomes exist regarding whether the transition to quantum-safe cryptography is completed across all legacy networks or if specific high-value chains are abandoned due to migration failures. A primary uncertainty is the exact timing and capability of quantum computers to break elliptic curve cryptography, which dictates the urgency of redesigning cryptographic protocols [3]. The necessity to implement catastrophic failure handlers to identify security breaches and prevent serious damage resists change even at this horizon, as the error cost of losing digital assets remains catastrophic [2][3].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may merge into a broader role of secure distributed systems engineering as blockchain-specific patterns become standardized components of general financial infrastructure.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may remain highly specialized as a distinct security discipline focused on the perpetual arms race between quantum decryption and post-quantum cryptographic verification.*

title: Computer Systems Engineers/Architects
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For computer systems architects broadly, the task of developing distributed system architectures is shifting toward the design of "AI factories," where the primary optimization metric moves from general storage and retrieval to the cost per token for inference throughput [10]. This broad architectural shift requires the integration of gigawatt-scale power and cooling infrastructure to support massive compute clusters [9] and the creation of specialized AI model customization pipelines to resolve performance gaps in base models [1]. For a subset of workers in organizations deploying agentic workloads, directing the analysis, development, and operation of complete computer systems may integrate risk intelligence frameworks to manage the unpredictable behaviors of autonomous agents [2][6]. In settings focused on high-performance inference, verifying the stability and scalability of system architecture now involves implementing tensor, context, and expert parallelism alongside optimized GPU communication protocols on non-proprietary platforms [3][4]. For architects in data center procurement contexts, identifying system hardware or software components includes evaluating open-standard AI chips and storage optimizations intended to deliver higher performance with a reduced physical hardware footprint [5][8]. For architects in regions prioritizing infrastructure autonomy, as reported in China, developing distributed system architectures involves the creation of massive card-based computing clusters to reduce dependency on foreign hardware stacks [7], while for those in regions implementing sovereign AI initiatives, as reported in the UK, the focus shifts toward designing supercomputing systems that prioritize reduced capital expenditure [11]. Directing the installation of network hardware is unlikely to change in the near term because it remains constrained by physical site requirements and manual verification protocols [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, computer systems architects may shift toward designing token-centric factory architectures and gigawatt-scale infrastructure, while subsegments integrate agentic risk governance and high-parallelism inference structures into their architectural operations.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the same architectural roles, if current trajectories hold, the task of designing and conducting hardware or software tests may expand to include the continuous validation of customized model performance under fluctuating operational loads [1]. For a subset of workers in organizations using autonomous workloads, extrapolating from current governance needs, the task of defining and analyzing objectives and organizational impact of information systems may incorporate specialized risk-intelligence parameters as a permanent architectural layer [2]. This shift assumes that agentic autonomy requires systemic governance integrated into the architecture rather than surface-level software configuration [2]. The requirement for documenting design specifications and installation instructions is likely to persist unchanged because human-readable blueprints remain necessary for regulatory auditability and long-term system maintenance [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the validation of domain-specific AI models and the architectural integration of agentic risk management may become routine tasks for a subset of systems architects.*

## Far (2046–2051)

Scope remains bounded to architectural design contexts. One rival outcome suggests that if model customization tools become fully commoditized, the need for architects to develop custom pipelines diminishes, shifting the focus back toward high-level system integration [1]. A competing outcome posits that hardware fragmentation between open-standard and proprietary stacks persists, requiring architects to maintain deep specialization in divergent hardware-software interfaces [8]. It remains unknown whether the energy requirements of gigawatt-scale centers will be mitigated by new materials or if they will create a permanent physical constraint on system scale [9]. The core task of verifying the interoperability and security of system architecture is expected to resist change, as these remain fundamental requirements regardless of the underlying compute paradigm.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the commoditization of AI customization may return the role's primary focus to high-level system integration and orchestration.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, persistent fragmentation between proprietary and open hardware stacks may force a permanent divergence in architectural specialization.*
