title: Intelligence Analysts
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of analysts specializing in cybercrime and critical infrastructure, and for analysts in intelligence agencies deploying agentic AI, the operational environment is shifting toward automated threat generation and synthesis [1][2][4]. Because AI-driven tools scale the volume of online fraud, analysts in cyber-focused subsegments must adjust how they analyze intelligence data to identify patterns and trends in criminal activity to isolate automated bot signatures from human-led scams [1]. In the context of national security, the targeting of energy and water infrastructure by state actors shifts the study of national security threats toward the specific analysis of programmable logic controllers (PLC) and SCADA systems [2]. The adoption of AI models capable of detecting cyber flaws may alter how these analysts identify gaps in information by automating the discovery of technical vulnerabilities in software [3]. Within specific organizations deploying AI "coworkers," the task of preparing comprehensive written reports is shifting from manual drafting to the management of AI agents that synthesize intelligence [4]. The task of interviewing, interrogating, or interacting with witnesses to collect human intelligence is unlikely to change in the near term because it depends on interpersonal trust and physical presence [5].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, analysts in these specific subsegments and organizations will face higher data noise from automated fraud and transition toward a supervisory role in AI-led report generation.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For analysts in these same subsegments and organizations, if current trajectories of agentic AI and state-sponsored cyber operations hold, the task of predicting future organized crime or terrorist activity may shift toward the analysis of competing algorithmic behaviors [1][2]. Extrapolating from early agent deployment, the task of preparing comprehensive written reports in specific intelligence agencies may evolve into the orchestration of multi-agent workflows, where the analyst defines the objective and validates the output [4]. As AI-generated synthetic data increases, the effort to evaluate records of communications could become more technically difficult, requiring specialized tools to distinguish human intent from bot-generated traffic [1][3]. The task of validating known intelligence with data from other sources is likely to persist as a human-led requirement because the catastrophic error cost of misattributing a state-sponsored attack necessitates rigorous human verification [5].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the core utility of manual communication analysis for these subsegments may decrease as the distinction between human and synthetic signals becomes more opaque.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For these subsegments and organizations, the possible emergence of adaptive, adversarial AI capable of real-time camouflage may render current pattern-recognition techniques obsolete. One plausible outcome is a shift toward a purely supervisory framework where analysts primarily manage AI systems that monitor other AI systems to identify anomalies [1][3]. A rival outcome is a strategic pivot back toward human intelligence and field observation as symbolic digital evidence becomes too easily manipulated by generative systems to be trusted [4][5]. The necessity of collaborating with representatives from other government and intelligence organizations will likely remain unchanged because jurisdictional boundaries and security clearances are structural constraints that resist automation [5]. It remains unknown whether a definitive technical solution for digital attribution can be achieved to resolve the ambiguity of AI-led attacks.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, analysts in these specific contexts may transition fully to a managerial role, orchestrating AI agents that handle the entirety of the technical analysis pipeline.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, these analysts may shift toward a higher reliance on non-digital human intelligence as AI-generated noise makes symbolic digital analysis fundamentally unreliable.*

title: Police and Sheriff's Patrol Officers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of officers in agencies adopting computer vision analytics, patrol operations may integrate real-time alerts regarding knives and suspect movement to support the task of monitoring, noting, reporting, and investigating suspicious persons and situations [1]. For patrol officers broadly, proposed limits on automated traffic safety cameras by the U.S. Department of Transportation may shift the task of monitoring traffic to ensure motorists observe traffic regulations back toward manual patrol stops [2]. These automated alerts do not replace the human requirement to review facts of incidents to determine if criminal act or statute violations were involved, as judicial standards for probable cause remain human-dependent [3]. The core task of identifying, pursuing, and arresting suspects is unlikely to change because algorithmic detection alone does not satisfy the legal requirements for seizure [3]. Physical apprehension procedures remain unchanged as they depend on officer discretion and tactile control in volatile environments [3].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, situational awareness may improve in specific jurisdictions using AI surveillance, while broader regulatory trends may increase the reliance on manual traffic enforcement.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

If current trajectories hold, the use of weapon detection software may expand within adopting agencies to prioritize calls based on AI-verified threats [1]. For the broader occupation, extrapolating from regulatory trends suggests a sustained reliance on manual traffic enforcement to replace restricted automated camera systems [2]. The task of evaluating complaint and emergency-request information to determine response requirements may incorporate algorithmic confidence scores alongside human assessment [3]. However, legal liability for false positives remains with the officer and the agency, which limits the potential for full reliance on automated systems. Standardized use-of-force protocols resist change because they are bound by state statutes and union contracts rather than vendor capabilities [3].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, workflow prioritization may shift toward AI-verified threats in adopting agencies, while manual traffic enforcement persists due to regulatory constraints on automation.*

## Far (2046–2051)

In agencies that integrated these tools, outcomes depend on the regulatory acceptance of algorithmic evidence. One outcome suggests that automated suspect tracking becomes a primary input for dispatch in urban districts to reduce response times for violent crimes [1]. A competing outcome posits that privacy litigation or public pushback restricts these tools to private security contexts rather than sworn law enforcement. It remains unknown whether courts will eventually accept AI-generated weapon detection as sufficient probable cause for an arrest [3]. The physical task of placing people in protective custody resists automation due to the need for real-time discretionary judgment in unpredictable human encounters [3].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, specific jurisdictions may standardize AI threat detection as a primary input for dispatch prioritization.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, legal challenges regarding data privacy may confine these technologies to non-sworn security roles or limited pilot programs.*

title: Customs and Border Protection Officers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For border officers in regions implementing digital border controls or labor exploitation research, such as the European Union and the United Kingdom, the workflow for examining immigration applications, visas, and passports is shifting toward digital-first verification [2]. The introduction of digital border control systems may alter the speed and interface of identity verification, although early deployment suggests potential for operational disruption [2]. Concurrently, research into the drivers of labor exploitation provides new evidence-based markers that may update the criteria used when interviewing persons to determine eligibility for admission [1]. Because the current evidence on labor exploitation is a review of findings, these updates likely remain at the level of experimental workflow adjustments and updated documentation of indicators rather than new legal mandates [1]. The task of locating and seizing contraband is unlikely to change in this period, as this remains dependent on physical inspection and sensor technology rather than documentation workflows [3].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, border officers in specific European jurisdictions may integrate digital verification systems and new evidence-based markers for labor exploitation into their primary screening and interviewing protocols.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For border officers in these same jurisdictional contexts, if current trajectories of digital adoption and evidence-based training hold, the task of interviewing persons to determine eligibility may shift from general identity verification toward a targeted diagnostic process [1][2]. Extrapolating from current deployment patterns, digital border systems may automate the routine aspects of examining passports, allowing officers to focus their social perceptiveness on higher-risk anomalies identified by the system [2]. The application of labor exploitation research may be operationalized into standardized behavioral markers used during admission interviews to identify victims of trafficking [1]. The requirement to testify regarding decisions in federal court is likely to persist unchanged because the legal accountability for detention and deportation requires human testimony and a traceable chain of judgment [3].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the interviewing process for admission may become a more specialized diagnostic function focused on risk anomalies and labor exploitation markers, provided digital systems stabilize.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For border officers in these specific regulatory environments, the detection of labor exploitation and documentation fraud may diverge into two rival outcomes. One possibility is that the analysis of immigration applications and visas becomes partially automated through predictive models, reducing the human interview's role to a secondary verification of system-flagged cases [2]. Alternatively, the detection of exploitation may remain a primarily qualitative human skill if the mechanisms used by exploiters evolve to bypass the systemic markers identified in current research [1]. It remains unknown whether the qualitative indicators of "decent work" can be computationally quantified with enough precision to replace human interviewing [1]. The physical act of detaining persons found to be in violation of laws will resist change because it necessitates the exercise of state-sanctioned physical force and legal authority [3].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the identification of potential labor exploitation and documentation errors may shift toward predictive analysis, narrowing the scope of the manual interview to exception handling.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, detection may remain a manual, qualitative interview process as exploitation methods adapt to evade automated systemic markers.*

title: Gambling Surveillance Officers and Gambling Investigators
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For the whole occupation broadly, the deployment of real-time computer vision tools for weapon detection and suspect tracking shifts the primary activity of observing casino operations for irregular activities from manual scanning to alert-based validation [1]. These tools may reduce the time spent on reviewing video surveillance footage by automatically stitching together the movement of specific individuals across multiple camera feeds [1][2]. This mechanism moves the officer's role toward a verification function rather than a discovery function. However, the task of reporting all violations and suspicious behaviors to supervisors is unlikely to change yet because regulatory gaming frameworks typically require a human agent to attest to the validity of a violation [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, surveillance officers shift from active visual searching to the validation of automated alerts for high-risk security threats.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

If current trajectories hold, the scope of automated detection may expand to include specific behavioral markers associated with cheating or theft, augmenting the task of monitoring establishment activities for adherence to gaming regulations [2]. This could move the officer's focus toward the higher-level analysis of complex patterns that the system flags as anomalous. The physical requirement to inspect and monitor audio or video surveillance equipment to ensure it is working appropriately remains unchanged because the underlying hardware depends on physical site maintenance [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation's core focus shifts from identifying individuals to analyzing the intent behind AI-flagged behavioral anomalies.*

## Far (2046–2051)

The scope remains centered on the surveillance of physical gambling sites, though the nature of the oversight may diverge. One outcome involves a transition where the primary role of the officer is solely the legal certification of AI-detected anomalies, acting as a regulatory signatory. A rival outcome is a regulatory mandate for "blind" human observation to mitigate the risk of automation bias, where officers must independently verify a subset of footage without AI assistance to ensure system integrity. The degree to which AI can identify nuanced, novel cheating methods—which often evolve in response to detection technology—remains an unknown variable. The necessity of acting as an oversight or security agent for management and customers persists due to the requirement for physical intervention in high-stakes environments [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the officer functions primarily as a legal auditor who certifies the accuracy of automated surveillance systems.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, regulatory requirements for human-only observation persist as a fail-safe against systemic automation bias.*

title: Security Guards
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For security guards in tech-adopting organizations, high-wealth residential settings, and specific regional retail environments, the deployment of specialized surveillance and shifting liability regimes are altering task workflows. In organizations adopting AI weapon detection, the task of answering alarms and investigating disturbances may shift from continuous manual visual scanning to the verification of software-generated alerts for knives and firearms [1]. For a subset of workers in high-wealth urban residential neighborhoods, the task of monitoring and authorizing entrance and departure may move toward responding to license plate analytics and virtual perimeter alerts [2]. In retail environments in regions where employee liability for intervention is strictly enforced, there may be increased demand for guards to specifically perform the task of apprehending or evicting violators to shield general retail staff from legal risk [3]. The use of suspect tracking tools could alter the workflow for those who patrol industrial or commercial premises by providing real-time location data on unauthorized persons [1]. Tasks involving the physical manipulation of hardware, such as locking doors and gates of entrances and exits, are unlikely to change in this horizon due to the absence of affordable, site-specific robotic actuators [4].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, security guards in specialized settings may transition to an alert-verification workflow for weapons and access control, while liability shifts in retail may increase the demand for professional enforcement roles.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the subset of workers in AI-augmented settings, the task of patrolling industrial or commercial premises may move from scheduled rounds to a reactive model driven by persistent suspect tracking signals [1]. Extrapolating from current residential deployments, the authorization of entrance and departure in high-wealth settings may become more dependent on automated database matches than on real-time human recognition [2]. If current trajectories hold, the role of the guard in retail environments may become more strictly decoupled from customer service, focusing primarily on the high-liability task of apprehending violators [3]. Despite these shifts, the requirement to warn persons of rule infractions persists because the legal authority to use force and the associated liability remain tied to human judgment [4]. The need for social perceptiveness when circulating among visitors to preserve order remains a stable constraint, as the nuance of human behavioral de-escalation resists algorithmic replication [4].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, patrolling and access control in high-technology settings may become primarily reactive to algorithmic signals, while enforcement and social management tasks remain human-centric.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For personnel in these AI-augmented environments, the long-term trajectory depends on whether regulatory frameworks prioritize individual privacy over surveillance efficiency [2]. One plausible outcome is that the task of inspecting and adjusting security systems is largely automated through self-diagnostic AI, narrowing the human role to high-level system auditing and emergency response [1]. A competing possibility is that sustained public resistance and restrictive privacy laws, similar to those debated in residential neighborhoods, restrict these tools to a small number of private facilities, leaving most guards reliant on manual observation [2]. It remains unknown whether AI can reliably differentiate between a threat and a non-threatening anomaly in highly unstructured environments without producing prohibitive false-positive rates [1]. Tasks such as escorting individuals to provide personal protection resist change due to the requirement for adaptive human response and physical presence [4].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, advanced analytics may automate the majority of system monitoring and inspection tasks within controlled environments, narrowing the human role to high-level auditing.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, restrictive privacy mandates may curtail the deployment of automated surveillance, preserving the manual nature of monitoring tasks across most organizational settings.*

title: Retail Loss Prevention Specialists
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For retail loss prevention specialists broadly, the deployment of computer vision systems capable of automated knife detection and suspect tracking modifies the execution of surveillance tasks [1]. Because these systems automate the identification of acute safety threats, the task of performing covert surveillance of areas susceptible to loss shifts from active visual scanning to the monitoring of automated alerts [1]. This technology alters the process of verifying proper functioning of physical security systems, as specialists must now calibrate detection parameters rather than simply ensuring camera uptime [1]. In regions where corporate liability risks discourage general staff from physical intervention, as observed in the United Kingdom [2], the task of apprehending shoplifters becomes more exclusively concentrated among loss prevention specialists to minimize organizational legal exposure [2]. Despite these shifts, the physical act of detention remains an embodied requirement governed by strict legal guidelines, making the core physicality of apprehension unlikely to change [3].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, AI-driven surveillance may reduce the cognitive load of manual monitoring, while corporate liability trends may narrow the pool of personnel authorized to perform physical apprehensions.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For retail loss prevention specialists broadly, if current trajectories in suspect tracking hold, the process of investigating known or suspected internal or external theft may shift toward the analysis of aggregated digital trajectories [1]. Instead of manually reviewing hours of footage, specialists could use AI-generated movement patterns to reconstruct theft events. The task of conducting store audits to identify problem areas may become more data-driven, relying on heatmaps of detected suspect activity to allocate physical patrols [1][3]. The requirement to collaborate with law enforcement agencies remains unchanged, as AI-generated alerts typically require human verification to meet the evidentiary standards for criminal reports [3].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may shift toward a hybrid role of security analyst and first responder, where manual surveillance is replaced by the validation of automated alerts.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For retail loss prevention specialists broadly, the long-term trajectory of automated surveillance presents rival outcomes depending on the evolution of privacy law. In one scenario, the integration of suspect tracking with automated access control could automate the task of inspecting buildings, equipment, or access points, limiting the specialist's role to incident response [1][3]. In a competing scenario, restrictive regulations on biometric tracking could render current suspect-tracking technologies obsolete, forcing a return to behavioral-based manual surveillance. It remains unknown whether legal frameworks will ever allow AI-triggered alerts to serve as the sole probable cause for apprehension. The task of testifying in civil or criminal court proceedings will likely resist automation, as the legal system requires a human witness to attest to the chain of custody and the specifics of an encounter [3].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may evolve into a specialized response role where most preventative monitoring is handled by an integrated autonomous security layer.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, regulatory constraints on surveillance may narrow the scope of AI tools, maintaining the specialist's role as the primary observer and investigator.*

title: Chefs and Head Cooks
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For chefs and head cooks broadly, operational focus is shifting toward the precision of menu design to ensure that dishes are executable for kitchen staff while maintaining cost standards [1]. This mechanism affects the task of collaborating with other personnel to plan and develop recipes or menus by prioritizing consistency and efficiency over purely creative output [1][2]. Similarly, the task of analyzing recipes to assign prices to menu items now requires a tighter integration of "little things" in operations to prevent margin erosion [1][2]. Because of the high physical variability in raw ingredients and the need for real-time sensorimotor adjustment, the core task of preparing and cooking foods is unlikely to change in this horizon [2]. 

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the role will emphasize the optimization of menu executability and cost-precision to maintain profitability.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For chefs and head cooks broadly, if current trajectories of operational optimization hold, the task of estimating amounts and costs of required supplies may become more dependent on granular data regarding recipe executability [1][2]. Extrapolating from current trends, the alignment between menu complexity and available staff skill levels could become a primary driver of production schedules and staff requirements [1][2]. The task of monitoring sanitation practices to ensure employees follow standards will likely persist unchanged due to the stability of health regulatory regimes [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, menu planning may increasingly function as a tool for labor-capacity management, where recipe design is constrained by the measured skill levels of the available workforce.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For chefs and head cooks broadly, the long-term trajectory of "executability" presents two rival outcomes. One path suggests a further narrowing of culinary variance to maximize operational efficiency, potentially reducing the chef's role to the orchestration of highly standardized systems. A competing path suggests a market correction where high-complexity, "inexecutable" menus become a luxury differentiator, restoring the emphasis on artisanal variance. It remains unknown whether labor market constraints or consumer preference will dictate the balance between standardization and complexity. Despite these shifts, the requirement to meet with customers to discuss menus for special occasions is likely to resist change due to the social and relational nature of high-end hospitality [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may evolve into a role focused on the operational orchestration of hyper-standardized, high-efficiency culinary systems.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, a premium on non-standardized, high-complexity culinary art may return the role to a focus on high-variance recipe development.*

title: First-Line Supervisors of Food Preparation and Serving Workers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For supervisors in organizations using performance-linked bonus structures for front-line staff, the introduction of quarterly bonuses tied to store metrics may alter how they evaluate workers and work procedures [1][2]. This mechanism likely shifts supervisory focus toward the specific key performance indicators (KPIs) required to trigger payouts, potentially increasing the frequency of monitoring to ensure compliance [2]. Because these bonuses are tied to store-wide results, supervisors may more aggressively recommend measures for improving work procedures to eliminate bottlenecks [2]. However, the requirement to train workers in sanitation and safety procedures is unlikely to change, as these tasks are governed by rigid health department regulations that outweigh internal performance incentives [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, supervisors in organizations with performance-based incentive programs may shift their evaluative focus toward KPI-driven monitoring of front-line workers.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For supervisors in these same incentive-driven organizations, if current trajectories hold, the role of analyzing operational problems, such as wastage, may become more tightly coupled with bonus eligibility [1][2]. Extrapolating from current incentive models, supervisors could prioritize the identification of specific inefficiencies that directly impact the metrics tied to financial rewards [2]. The task of assigning duties and work stations to employees will likely persist as a real-time, manual coordination activity due to the high variability of customer flow in food service environments [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, supervisors in organizations using performance bonuses may adopt more rigorous, data-centric methods for analyzing operational problems to ensure the achievement of store metrics.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For supervisors in organizations using performance-linked incentives, the long-term evolution of the role remains uncertain depending on how metrics are tracked. If performance monitoring becomes fully automated, the supervisory role may shift primarily toward resolving customer complaints and managing interpersonal conflicts, as the technical evaluation of "performance" moves to software [2]. Conversely, if the pressure of metric-driven bonuses leads to high worker turnover, supervisors may shift their focus back toward intensive personnel training and retention strategies to maintain a baseline operational capacity [2]. The necessity of presenting bills and accepting payments, or overseeing these tasks, resists change as long as the point-of-sale remains the primary interface for financial transaction finalization [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, automated performance tracking may reduce the supervisory burden of worker evaluation, shifting the role's core toward emotional labor and conflict resolution.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, extreme metric-driven pressure may force a supervisory shift toward high-touch personnel support and retention to counteract systemic burnout.*


## References

title: Cooks, Fast Food
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

In regions with high minimum wage mandates, such as California, the financial viability of fast food operations may be constrained. Increased labor costs associated with core tasks—such as operating large-volume cooking equipment [2] and cooking items ordered by customers [2]—can lead to significant operating expenses that may result in business insolvency for some franchisees [1]. This economic pressure may reduce job stability for cooks in these specific regulatory environments [1]. Because the existing installed base of cooking equipment is specialized for limited menus, the fundamental physical methods of food preparation are unlikely to change in the immediate term [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, cooks in high-wage regions may face increased employment instability as some franchise operations become financially unsustainable.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

In the same high-wage regional contexts, if current trajectories of labor cost increases hold, firms may attempt to reduce the headcount required to cook and package batches of food [2]. Extrapolating from current financial pressures, this may drive a transition toward more automated cooking systems to lower the per-unit labor cost of preparation [1]. However, the requirement to maintain sanitation, health, and safety standards in work areas [2] is likely to persist as a human-centric task due to the high cost of automating deep-cleaning and sanitation verification.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, labor-cost pressures in specific regions may lead to a reduction in human labor for batch-cooking tasks through the adoption of automated equipment.*

## Far (2046–2051)

In high-wage regulatory environments, the long-term survival of the limited-menu fast food model remains unknown. One plausible outcome is the near-complete automation of the cooking process, where humans are only retained to verify that prepared food meets requirements for quality and quantity [2]. A rival outcome involves a structural shift in the business model toward higher-priced offerings to absorb labor costs, maintaining the human cook's role in preparing specialty foods [2]. Even at this horizon, the physical constraint of managing waste—such as taking out garbage—resists automation due to the unstructured nature of waste disposal environments.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the cooking function in high-wage regions may shift almost entirely to automated systems, with humans relegated to quality oversight.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may persist through a shift to premium pricing models that sustain human labor for specialty food preparation.*

title: Bartenders
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For bartenders broadly, consumer tipping fatigue may reduce the frequency and volume of gratuities processed during the task of collecting money for drinks served [1]. For bartenders in the United States, revised IRS deduction rules may alter the administrative recording and reporting requirements involved in balancing cash receipts [2]. In specific urban municipalities where tip credits are legally contested, the mechanism for calculating base wages relative to gratuities may shift [3]. These factors collectively may introduce higher volatility in net take-home pay while increasing the regulatory precision required for financial tasks [1][2][3]. The task of checking identification of customers to verify age requirements is unlikely to change because it is governed by binding legal mandates and liquor licensing regimes [4]. Similarly, the physical process of mixing ingredients to prepare cocktails remains stable as it relies on established recipe standards and manual dexterity [4].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, bartenders may experience a decline in discretionary earnings and increased regional variability in wage structures due to shifting consumer behaviors and regulatory adjustments.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For bartenders broadly, if current trajectories of tipping fatigue persist, the mechanism for collecting money for drinks served may shift toward structured service charges or modified payment models to stabilize labor income [1]. This shift would occur because a reliance on discretionary gratuities may become an insufficient incentive for labor retention in high-fatigue consumer environments [1]. Such a transition would depend on the ability of establishments to implement service fees without alienating price-sensitive patrons [1]. The task of stocking the bar with beer, wine, liquor, and related supplies is unlikely to change because it depends on low-cost manual coordination and the existing physical architecture of bar layouts [4].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the compensation structure for bartenders may move away from discretionary tipping toward more stabilized, organization-led payment mechanisms.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For bartenders broadly, the economic model of the occupation may diverge based on the service environment. In one scenario, the role could transition to a standardized wage model as discretionary tipping ceases to be a viable primary income source across most settings [1][3]. In a competing scenario, tipping may persist exclusively in luxury settings where gratuities function as a social signal of status rather than a standard service fee. It remains unknown whether the tax frameworks for digital payments and tip deductions [2] will evolve into a global standard or remain fragmented by jurisdiction. The task of attempting to limit problems and liability related to customers' excessive drinking will likely resist change because it requires real-time social perceptiveness and the management of unpredictable human behavior [4].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may shift toward a standardized hourly wage model across most service settings.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may bifurcate into a market where tipping survives only in high-end, luxury environments.*

title: Fast Food and Counter Workers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of workers in drive-thru operations, the deployment of voice AI is automating the task of requesting and recording customer orders [3][4][5]. In regions where high mandatory minimum wages create severe financial pressure on franchisees, as reported in California, this automation may be accelerated as a mechanism to reduce labor costs [2]. For the occupation broadly, a professional debate has emerged regarding whether the prioritization of operational efficiency is eroding the empathy required when communicating with customers regarding orders, comments, and complaints [1]. Because this signal is primarily a critique of industry trends, the near-term effect is likely limited to shifts in performance evaluation criteria and service standards rather than operational mandates [1]. Tasks involving performing cleaning duties and preparing daily food items are unlikely to change because they require physical dexterity and adherence to sanitary measures that current automation cannot reliably execute [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the occupation sees a targeted reduction in human voice-interaction tasks within drive-thru subsegments, while the broader workforce faces a tension between efficiency-driven metrics and service empathy.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For workers in drive-thru subsegments, if current trajectories of voice automation hold, the human role may shift from primary data entry to managing system exceptions and error resolution [3][4][5]. Extrapolating from current discourse on efficiency, the task of communicating with customers regarding complaints may become the primary human-facing responsibility, as routine transactions are decoupled from human labor [1]. In high-wage regions, this transition may be more pronounced if financial pressures continue to drive the replacement of entry-level transaction roles [2]. The requirement to clean and organize eating, service, and kitchen areas will likely persist unchanged due to the high variability of physical debris and the necessity of human oversight for food safety compliance [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the subsegment of drive-thru workers may transition into a role focused on service recovery and system oversight, while routine order-taking is handled by automated interfaces.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For workers in automated fast-service settings, the long-term structure of the role depends on whether the market values hospitality as a technical output or a uniquely human service [1]. One plausible outcome is that the human role is reduced almost entirely to embodied tasks, such as scrubbing and polishing counters, as simulated empathy in AI satisfies basic customer needs [1][3][4][5]. A competing outcome suggests that as automation becomes ubiquitous, human interaction may be re-established as a premium differentiator, shifting the occupation toward a high-touch hospitality model [1]. It remains unknown whether the task of preparing simple foods can be fully automated without compromising safety, but the necessity of monitoring food temperatures and maintaining sanitary measures will likely resist complete automation due to the catastrophic error cost of foodborne illness [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may be reduced to a facility maintenance and sanitation role, with all transaction and order-taking tasks fully automated.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may pivot toward a specialized hospitality role where human interaction is a premium feature used to differentiate luxury fast-service brands.*

title: Baristas
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For baristas in large-scale coffee organizations using centralized performance-tracking systems, compensation may incorporate quarterly bonuses tied to specific store-level metrics [1][2]. This mechanism shifts the incentive structure for tasks such as prepare or serve hot or cold beverages, where throughput speed and efficiency may now directly influence total earnings [2]. The implementation of such bonuses likely depends on the use of point-of-sale data gathered while workers receive and process customer payments to measure store performance [2]. These incentives may alter the internal prioritization of tasks, potentially favoring speed over the time spent to describe menu items to customers [2]. However, the physical requirements of the role, such as clean or sanitize work areas, are unlikely to change as they remain mandated by health and safety regulations [3].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, baristas in specific high-volume corporate settings may experience a transition toward variable, metric-driven compensation models.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

If current trajectories hold, performance-based incentive structures may propagate to other large-scale coffee chains competing for labor in similar market segments [1][2]. This diffusion would likely remain confined to organizations with the necessary digital infrastructure to monitor store-level performance metrics in real-time [2]. Extrapolating from recent corporate deployments, independent cafes are unlikely to adopt these specific bonus models due to a lack of standardized metrics and a different focus on artisanal customer interaction [3]. Routine embodied tasks, such as stock customer service stations with paper products, will persist unchanged due to their low complexity and lack of measurable "speed" benefit [3].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, metric-linked bonuses may become a competitive standard for labor attraction and retention among large corporate coffee operators.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For workers in large-scale corporate coffee environments, one possibility involves the integration of sensor-based monitoring to automate the tracking of tasks like prepare or serve hot or cold beverages for real-time pay calculations [1][2]. A competing outcome is that labor regulations or collective bargaining agreements could prohibit variable pay tied to speed, reverting compensation to fixed hourly rates to prevent worker burnout [2]. It remains unknown whether the technical nuance of specialty beverage preparation will be fully automated or remain a human-led craft. Regardless of the compensation model, the requirement to take out garbage and perform basic facility maintenance will likely resist automation due to the high variability of the physical environment [3].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, large organizations may implement high-precision automated monitoring to tightly couple compensation with per-second task efficiency.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, regulatory interventions may decouple wages from performance metrics to protect worker well-being in high-volume settings.*

title: Waiters and Waitresses
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For waiters and waitresses broadly, the adoption of efficiency-focused digital tools may shift the interaction model from hospitality-driven to transactional [1]. As automated systems streamline the task of entering orders into computers, the interpersonal depth required when taking orders from patrons for food or beverages may diminish [1]. Simultaneously, emerging consumer tipping fatigue may reduce the financial incentive for servers to prioritize high-empathy tasks, such as checking with customers to ensure they are enjoying their meals [2]. For servers in the United States, updated tax regulations regarding deductions for tips may alter the administrative overhead associated with collecting payments from customers [3]. In US metropolitan areas where legislative efforts to eliminate tip credits are active, the decoupling of base wages from gratuities may shift the economic incentive structure of the role [4]. The task of removing dishes and glasses from tables is unlikely to change in this horizon, as the capital cost of deploying robotics capable of navigating unstructured dining environments remains higher than the cost of manual labor [5].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the role may shift toward a more transactional function as efficiency tools reduce interaction depth and declining tipping incentives diminish the emphasis on high-touch hospitality.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For waiters and waitresses broadly, if current trajectories toward transactional efficiency and tipping volatility hold, the occupation may bifurcate based on the priced value of empathy. Extrapolating from the tension between operational efficiency and hospitality [1], low-cost dining segments may further automate the tasks of presenting menus and answering questions about menu items to reduce labor costs [5]. In contrast, high-end establishments may explicitly price human hospitality as a premium service to decouple worker income from volatile consumer tipping behavior [2]. The requirement to check patrons' identification to ensure they meet minimum age requirements for alcohol consumption will likely persist as a human-mediated task to manage legal liability and regulatory compliance [5].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may split into low-cost transactional roles focused on logistics and high-touch roles where empathy is treated as a priced luxury.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For waiters and waitresses broadly, the persistence of human staffing depends on the cost-convergence of humanoid robotics for embodied tasks. One plausible outcome is a systemic reduction in human presence where workers only intervene to correct any problems or handle complex social exceptions that automation cannot resolve [5]. A rival outcome is a market-driven resurgence in human-centric service as a reaction against total automation, where the hospitality factor [1] is restored as the primary value proposition of the dining experience. It remains unknown whether robotics will achieve the necessary site variability to reliably handle the task of cleaning tables or counters across diverse and changing restaurant layouts [5].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, human servers may be relegated to exception handlers who manage only the failures of an otherwise automated transactional system.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, a market correction may drive a resurgence in human-led hospitality, repositioning the server as a specialist in emotional labor.*

title: Landscaping and Groundskeeping Workers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For landscaping and groundskeeping workers broadly, the availability of effective robot mowers may reduce the manual hours spent to mow or edge lawns [1][2]. Because autonomous systems can now reliably operate powered equipment for turf maintenance [1][2], the physical demand of repetitive mowing tasks decreases [1]. This shift is likely confined to flat, established turf areas where navigation is predictable. The task to plant seeds, bulbs, foliage, or shrubs [2] is unlikely to change yet because the fine motor skills and site-specific judgment required for planting in unstructured soil exceed current robotic capabilities.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, automation may reduce the manual labor hours required for basic turf maintenance across the occupation.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For landscaping and groundskeeping workers broadly, if current trajectories in robotic turf maintenance hold, labor allocation may shift toward more complex horticultural tasks [1]. As the requirement to operate vehicles or powered equipment for basic mowing declines, workers may spend a greater proportion of their time to prune or trim trees, shrubs, or hedges [2], which require higher precision and vertical reach. The task to gather and remove litter [2] persists unchanged due to the high variability of debris types and the unpredictable nature of litter placement in outdoor environments.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may shift toward a specialty role where basic turf cutting is handled by autonomous systems, increasing the relative importance of pruning and detailed plant care.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For landscaping and groundskeeping workers broadly, long-term outcomes depend on whether robotics evolve from single-task mowers to multi-purpose land managers. In one scenario, the occupation focuses on the high-aesthetic requirement to decorate gardens with stones or plants [2], overseeing fleets of maintenance robots. In a rival scenario, a shift toward ecological restoration and biodiversity mandates may render autonomous mowing less relevant, prioritizing manual soil and habitat management. It remains unknown whether sensors can reliably distinguish between invasive species and desired ground covers in complex, non-standardized landscapes. The task to shovel snow from walks and driveways [2] resists change due to the extreme variability of snow accumulation and the high-torque physical force required for clearance.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may transition into a fleet-management and high-end aesthetic design role.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may pivot toward ecological land management and restoration, emphasizing manual biodiversity interventions over automated maintenance.*


## References

title: Gambling Dealers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

In regions where U.S. tax regulations apply, the expansion of tip deduction rules may alter how dealers manage the administrative aspects of their compensation [1]. This change specifically affects tasks involving paying winnings or collecting bets [1] and the recording of patrons' cash wagers [1], as dealers must now account for digital payments and automatic gratuities under clarified IRS guidelines [1]. Because these regulations focus on the tax treatment of gratuities, the administrative burden of tracking these payments may increase for the worker [1]. The physical act of dealing cards to players (Task 7) is unlikely to change in this period because the tactile and social nature of live gaming remains the primary value proposition for casino patrons.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, dealers in the U.S. will experience a shift in how they document and report digital gratuities due to updated tax deduction frameworks.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

In regions with similar tax regimes to the U.S., if current trajectories toward digital payment formalization hold, the process of recording patrons' cash wagers (Task 9) may become increasingly integrated with automated tax-reporting systems [1]. This transition could reduce the manual effort required for dealers to track eligible tips for deduction purposes [1]. The necessity of greeting customers and making them feel welcome (Task 2) will likely persist, as the social-emotional labor of the role is a non-computable element of the gaming experience.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the administrative tracking of tips for dealers in these regions may shift from manual recording to automated, tax-compliant digital systems.*

## Far (2046–2051)

In regions where digital gratuity tracking has been standardized, the long-term impact of tax-integrated payment systems remains uncertain. One possibility is that the recording of winnings and losses (Task 13) becomes entirely decoupled from the dealer's manual input, handled instead by embedded table sensors and direct-to-tax digital ledgers [1]. A rival outcome is that increased regulatory scrutiny of digital tips leads to more rigid, audited reporting requirements that constrain how dealers interact with patrons during the exchange of currency (Task 3). Regardless of the reporting mechanism, the requirement to inspect cards and equipment for condition (Task 5) will likely resist change to ensure game integrity and prevent fraud.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, tip and wager reporting for dealers in these regions may become an invisible, fully automated background process integrated into the gaming table infrastructure.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the formalization of digital gratuities may lead to highly restrictive regulatory protocols that diminish the dealer's autonomy in managing table-side currency exchanges.*


## References

title: First-Line Supervisors of Retail Sales Workers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

In organizations utilizing AI agents for store management, the scope of supervisory work may shift toward managing the interface between automated systems and human staff. These agents may begin to automate symbolic tasks such as inventorying stock and reordering when levels drop [2] or planning and preparing work schedules [2]. However, early deployments indicate that agents may struggle with the interpersonal requirements of directing and supervising employees [2], specifically regarding the consistency of staff coordination and memory of personnel needs [1]. Consequently, the human supervisor's role in these specific settings may move toward correcting agent-driven scheduling or coordination errors [1]. Instructing staff on how to handle difficult and complicated sales [2] is unlikely to change in the near term because it requires high-order social perceptiveness and real-time nuance that current agent deployments lack.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, supervisors in organizations adopting management agents will see a reduction in symbolic administrative tasks but an increase in the need to mediate conflicts between automated agent directives and human staff requirements.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

In organizations employing advanced management agents, if current trajectories hold, the division of labor may bifurcate between "logistical supervision" and "personnel supervision." Agents may manage the majority of tasks related to reviewing inventory and sales records to prepare reports [2] and examining merchandise for correct pricing [2]. The human supervisor may be relegated to the purely interpersonal aspects of the role, such as evaluating personnel [2] or responding to complex customer complaints [2]. Enforcing safety, health, and security rules [2] likely persists as a human-led activity due to the requirement for physical presence and legal accountability for workplace safety.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, for a subset of supervisors in AI-integrated stores, the role may shift from general coordination to a specialized focus on human performance and emotional labor management.*

## Far (2046–2051)

In stores utilizing mature management agents, the extent of human supervisory necessity remains unknown, depending on whether agents can resolve the failure to maintain stable human staff relations seen in early deployments [1]. One possibility is that agents achieve bounded autonomy over all symbolic and logistical tasks, including estimating consumer demand [2] and formulating pricing policies [2], leaving the human supervisor as a purely cultural or brand ambassador. A rival outcome is that the friction between agent-driven efficiency and human staff retention leads some organizations to revert to human-centric lean management to avoid the personnel volatility associated with algorithmic supervision [1]. Providing customer service by greeting and assisting customers [2] in high-touch environments will likely resist total automation due to the continued value of human social signaling.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, for supervisors in highly automated settings, the role may evolve into a personnel coach who manages human staff's psychological well-being while the agent handles all operational logic.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the failures of agent-based personnel management may lead to a resurgence of traditional human supervisors who prioritize staff stability over algorithmic optimization.*


## References

1. Fast Company (2026-04-14). "An AI agent opened a store in San Francisco. Then it forgot the staff." https://www.fastcompany.com/91526099/andon-market-san-francisco-ai-store
2. O*NET OnLine (2024). Task Statements for 41-1011.00. U.S. Department of Labor. https://www.onetonline.org/link/summary/41-1011.00

title: Cashiers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

In organizations deploying specialized AI assistants, the scope of the cashier's role may narrow as automated platforms take over specific informational tasks. Because platforms can now handle inquiries regarding POS operations, maintenance, and payments [1], the frequency with which workers must provide information on procedures or policies (O*NET Task 8) and resolve customer complaints (O*NET Task 4) may decrease. This shift moves the cashier from the primary point of procedural resolution to a secondary supervisor of the AI's output. However, tasks requiring tactile manipulation, such as bagging, boxing, or wrapping merchandise (O*NET Task 26), are unlikely to change in these settings because AI assistants lack the physical embodiment required for material handling.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, a subset of cashiers in organizations using AI assistants may experience a reduction in the cognitive load associated with processing routine procedural inquiries.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For cashiers in small-format retail environments, if current trajectories hold, the use of AI assistants for POS-related troubleshooting may migrate from individual early-adopting organizations to a broader class of similar retail settings [1]. This could lead to a further atrophy of the need for cashiers to answer customers' questions (O*NET Task 8) as automated systems standardize the delivery of operational information. Despite this, the requirement to maintain clean and orderly checkout areas (O*NET Task 12) persists, as AI software cannot perform the physical cleaning duties required for site hygiene.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the role of cashiers in small-format retail may shift further toward physical facility maintenance and complex transaction oversight if AI assistants standardize procedural support.*

## Far (2046–2051)

In the subsegment of retail environments utilizing integrated AI assistants, the trajectory of the occupation remains uncertain due to a tension between automation and the error costs of financial disputes. One plausible outcome is that the task of resolving complaints (O*NET Task 4) is almost entirely automated, leaving the human worker to focus primarily on physical security and inventory. A rival outcome is that the high friction associated with payment errors [1] creates a renewed demand for human-centric validation for all non-standard transactions. The task of greeting customers entering establishments (O*NET Task 2) may resist change even at this horizon, provided that social norms continue to prioritize human interaction during the initial point of entry in physical commerce.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, cashiers in AI-integrated environments may evolve into physical site stewards whose primary function is security and inventory management.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, cashiers may see a resurgence in the importance of social perceptiveness as AI assistants handle all routine tasks, leaving only high-emotion conflict resolution to the human worker.*


## References

1. Cstore Dive (2026). "Loop Neighborhood Market deploys AI assistant." https://www.cstoredive.com/news/loop-neighborhood-market-deploys-ai-assistant/816631/

title: Retail Salespersons
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For retail salespersons broadly, the availability of AI-driven digital interfaces may reduce the human associate's role in basic information retrieval. Because customers can scan QR codes to receive instant answers about product specifications [1], the task of answering questions regarding merchandise may shift toward automated systems. This mechanism could similarly affect how workers describe merchandise and explain its use to customers [1]. Consequently, recommending merchandise based on customer needs may become a shared task between the worker and an AI advisor [1]. Tasks requiring physical presence and manual dexterity, such as cleaning shelves, counters, and tables, are unlikely to change as they lack a digital equivalent [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, basic product information retrieval and initial needs assessment may shift from human associates to AI-driven digital interfaces in physical retail environments.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For retail salespersons broadly, if current trajectories hold, the occupation may transition from being the primary source of product knowledge to acting as a curator of AI-generated options. Extrapolating from the deployment of digital advisors [1], the task of recommending merchandise may evolve into validating AI suggestions for the customer. The human associate could focus more on the physical preparation of merchandise for purchase or rental, which remains a manual process [2]. The core requirement to watch for and recognize security risks is likely to persist unchanged because of the unpredictable nature of physical theft and the need for human judgment in conflict resolution [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may move toward a hybrid model where AI handles data-driven recommendations while humans manage physical fulfillment and store security.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For retail salespersons broadly, the long-term structure of the occupation depends on the potential integration of embodied robotics into the sales floor. One rival outcome is that high-value retail remains a human-centric experience to maintain a luxury signal, while budget retail becomes fully automated. Another uncertainty is whether AI can eventually perform the task of inventorying stock and requisitioning new stock without human oversight [2]. Even at this horizon, the task of handling complex returns and exchanges may resist full automation due to the nuanced social negotiation required to resolve customer disputes [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may bifurcate into high-touch specialized consultation for luxury goods and low-touch logistics management for automated stores.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, widespread adoption of embodied robotics may automate both the information and the physical handling tasks, reducing the human role to a minimal supervisory presence.*


## References

1. Pymnts (2026). "AI Is the New Sales Associate in Physical Retail." https://www.pymnts.com/news/retail/2026/ai-is-the-new-sales-associate-in-physical-retail/

title: Advertising Sales Agents
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of advertising sales agents managing inventory on AI platforms, the adoption of dedicated ads manager tools may automate the process of providing clients with estimates of costs [3] and processing paperwork related to accounts [8] [1]. This technology shifts the mechanism of preparing promotional plans and sales literature [7] from manual document creation to platform-driven configuration [1]. Because these tools standardize the offering of AI-native ad placements, the time spent on recommending appropriate sizes and formats [12] is likely to decrease for this subsegment. However, the delivery of sales presentations to new customers [1] is unlikely to change, as the acquisition of high-spend accounts still requires interpersonal persuasion and high-context negotiation.

*Hypothesis: For a subset of agents specializing in AI platforms, administrative tasks and cost estimation will be partially automated by platform-native tools in the near term.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the same subset of workers in AI-platform sales, if current trajectories hold, the task of locating and contacting potential clients [4] may shift toward managing algorithmic lead-generation feeds provided by the ads manager [1]. The mechanism for preparing sample advertisements within the selected medium [14] could become largely autonomous, reducing the agent's role to a reviewer of AI-generated proofs [10]. Despite these shifts, obtaining and studying information about clients' business practices to offer effective sales presentations [6] will likely persist as a human-led task due to the requirement for deep qualitative alignment with a client's long-term business strategy.

*Hypothesis: For a subset of agents in AI-platform sales, the role may shift from manual prospecting and sampling toward the oversight of algorithmic lead generation and automated proofing in the mid term.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For the subset of agents specializing in AI-mediated media, the role may diverge based on the evolution of B2B procurement. In one scenario, the task of preparing sample advertisements [14] and determining the advertising medium [14] becomes entirely autonomous, shifting the agent's focus exclusively to high-level consultation with company officials to develop promotional plans [16] [1]. In a competing scenario, the requirement for a human agent to study client needs [6] may be superseded by AI-to-AI negotiation between the advertiser's procurement system and the platform's ads manager [1]. It remains unknown whether the "ads manager" will continue to function as a tool for the agent or evolve into a replacement for the transactional agent. The final legal approval of contracts [9] is likely to resist full automation due to the necessity of human accountability in high-value corporate agreements.

*Hypothesis A: For a subset of agents in AI-platform sales, the role evolves into a high-level strategic consultancy focused on organizational alignment in the far term.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): For a subset of agents in AI-platform sales, the role is eliminated as AI-to-AI procurement systems automate the entire lifecycle from lead generation to contract approval in the far term.*

title: Insurance Sales Agents
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For agents in the brokerage subsegment, administrative friction remains a primary constraint during the submission process. The process of performing administrative tasks [2], specifically the assembly of new submissions, is hindered by fragmented data across emails and attachments [1]. This bottleneck slows the ability to contact underwriters and submit forms to obtain binder coverage [2] because agents must manually rename documents and identify missing information [1]. Consequently, the time required to customize insurance programs [2] is extended by the need to manually synthesize scattered client details [1]. The requirement to interview prospective clients to obtain data about financial resources and physical conditions [2] is unlikely to change yet due to the high error cost associated with inaccurate risk assessment.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, agents in brokerage settings will continue to experience significant productivity bottlenecks in the administrative tasks related to policy submissions.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For agents in the brokerage subsegment, if current trajectories toward better document orchestration hold, the mechanism of data ingestion may shift. Extrapolating from current bottlenecks in submission handling [1], the task of maintaining records and handling policy renewals [2] could move from manual document assembly to the oversight of automated synthesis tools. This shift may reduce the time spent on the low-value administrative components of contacting underwriters [2]. However, the need to explain features, advantages, and disadvantages of various policies [2] will likely persist unchanged because this task relies on persuasion and social perceptiveness to align complex products with client needs [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the administrative burden of submission assembly for brokerage agents may decrease as automated data synthesis reduces manual document handling.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For agents in the brokerage subsegment, the long-term evolution of the submission process depends on whether data standardization occurs across the insurance ecosystem. One outcome is the total elimination of the submission bottleneck through real-time, standardized data exchange between clients and underwriters. A rival outcome is that administrative friction persists or increases because regulatory requirements for documentation become more granular and complex. The core task of coordinating between clients and underwriters to obtain coverage [2] will likely resist full automation due to the necessity of negotiating bespoke terms for non-standard risks. It remains unknown whether the brokerage model will survive if the friction of "customizing programs" [2] is entirely removed.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, standardized data ecosystems eliminate the administrative bottleneck in brokerage submissions, shifting the agent's role almost entirely to risk advisory.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, increasing regulatory complexity maintains or increases the administrative burden of policy submissions despite advances in automation.*


## References

title: Securities, Commodities, and Financial Services Sales Agents
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of workers in the mortgage lending subsegment, the adoption of AI pre-underwriting tools may shift the nature of initial client interactions [1]. As AI automates the verification of documents and initial risk assessments, the task of interviewing clients to determine assets and liabilities may shift from manual data collection to the validation of AI-generated summaries [2]. This transition moves the operational focus toward customer success roles that manage the output of these tools rather than performing the primary data review [1]. The task of reviewing transactions to ensure conformance to governing agency regulations is unlikely to change significantly in the near term because of the high error cost and legal liability associated with lending mandates [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, agents in the mortgage subsegment may see a shift in task allocation where AI manages initial risk data and humans focus on managing the client's experience through the automated pipeline.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the same subset of mortgage-focused agents: if current trajectories hold, AI tools could expand from pre-underwriting to the preliminary generation of tailored loan proposals. This may alter the process of preparing proposals to sell services that address client needs by automating the matching of loan products to AI-verified financial profiles [2]. The core task of discussing financial options with clients will likely persist unchanged, as the high-stakes nature of home financing requires trust and nuanced negotiation to resolve client anxieties [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the role for mortgage-focused agents may transition toward a hybrid of customer success and final-stage negotiation, with AI handling the majority of the proposal construction.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For agents within the mortgage lending niche: the long-term trajectory depends on whether regulatory bodies permit autonomous final approvals. If autonomous systems are permitted, the role may transition entirely into a platform-management function where the agent oversees the interface between the client and the software [1]. Conversely, if liability laws continue to mandate a human signatory for all financial commitments, the agent's role may consolidate around final risk certification and high-level relationship management for complex cases [2]. It remains unknown whether AI can accurately model the idiosyncratic risk of non-standard borrowers. The requirement for a licensed professional to assume legal responsibility for financial advice is likely to resist change even at this horizon [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, mortgage sales agents in this subsegment may evolve into customer success managers for fully automated lending platforms.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the role may narrow into a specialized "risk certifier" role where the human agent provides the final legal sign-off on AI-generated loan approvals.*

title: Sales Representatives of Services, Except Advertising, Insurance, Financial Services, and Travel
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of workers in hotel group sales, AI-powered revenue management tools may alter how representatives quote prices, credit terms, contract terms, or fulfillment dates for services [1][2]. Because these tools provide real-time yield optimization for bulk room blocks, the mechanism for deciding rates shifts from static pricing lists to algorithmic suggestions [1]. This specifically affects the ability to negotiate prices or terms of sales or service agreements, as representatives rely on data-driven constraints to maximize revenue [1][2]. It is unlikely that representatives will stop the need to distribute promotional materials at meetings, conferences, or trade shows, as these tasks require physical presence and social signaling in high-touch environments [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, a subset of hospitality sales representatives will use algorithmic yield data to inform their pricing and negotiation tasks.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For this same subset of hospitality sales representatives, if current trajectories in revenue management hold, the task to compute and compare costs of services may be largely subsumed by automated systems [1][2]. Extrapolating from the current use of AI in group bookings, the representative's role could shift from manual calculation to the oversight of algorithmic outputs [1]. Despite this, the requirement to consult with clients after sales or contract signings to resolve problems and provide ongoing support is likely to persist, as conflict resolution in service contracts involves unstructured interpersonal coordination [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, cost computation for hotel group sales will move toward automated oversight, while post-sale relationship management remains a human-led activity.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For representatives in the group hospitality subsegment, the degree to which bulk purchasers accept non-negotiable algorithmic pricing remains an unresolvable uncertainty. One plausible outcome is that standard group booking negotiations are fully handled by autonomous systems, removing the representative from the pricing loop for all but the most complex contracts. However, the need to maintain customer records using automated systems will resist change, as the administrative requirement for a system of record is fundamental to the business model [2]. A rival outcome exists where high-value luxury segments reject algorithmic pricing in favor of bespoke, human-negotiated terms to maintain a sense of exclusivity.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, standard group service negotiations are automated, restricting human representatives to high-complexity or high-value exceptions.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, a divergence emerges where prestige service segments mandate human-led negotiation to signal luxury and exclusivity, resisting algorithmic pricing.*


## References

title: Real Estate Brokers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For real estate brokers broadly, the integration of AI assistants is shifting the allocation of time away from administrative overhead toward strategic client advisory. Automated systems now handle lead intake and CRM updates, reducing the manual effort required to generate lists of properties and their descriptions [1]. The deployment of call coaching tools may alter how brokers act as an intermediary in negotiations between buyers and sellers by providing real-time feedback on communication patterns [1]. Simultaneously, the broker's role as a market analyst is emphasized as they must actively counter client misconceptions regarding interest rates and market timing to prevent buyers from remaining on the sidelines [2]. The use of AI for offer drafting is emerging, though the broker must still monitor fulfillment of purchase contract terms to ensure legal compliance [1]. Licensing requirements and fiduciary duties are unlikely to change in this period because statutory liability for transaction errors remains tied to the individual license holder.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, administrative tasks are partially automated, shifting the broker's primary value proposition toward strategic market advisory and high-stakes negotiation coaching.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For real estate brokers broadly, if current trajectories hold, the role may shift further from data aggregation toward complex behavioral economics and market psychology. Extrapolating from current advisory trends, brokers may rely on predictive analytics to compare a property with similar properties that have recently sold, using this data to steer clients through volatile interest rate environments [2]. The process of giving buyers virtual tours may become a standardized baseline, moving the broker's focus from property access to the interpretation of property potential [1]. Despite these shifts, the need to maintain awareness of current income tax regulations and local zoning remains stable because these tasks require site-specific human judgment and professional liability that AI cannot assume. The management of real estate offices will likely focus on the orchestration of these AI-driven lead flows rather than the manual supervision of agent paperwork.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, valuation and market analysis become data-driven commodities, increasing the premium on the broker's ability to provide psychological reassurance and strategic timing advice.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For real estate brokers broadly, rival outcomes emerge regarding the automation of the closing process. One plausible trajectory suggests that arranging for title searches and checking work completed by loan officers becomes fully integrated into autonomous digital transaction ecosystems [1]. A competing trajectory suggests that strict liability regimes and the high cost of errors in property law force a permanent human "circuit breaker" into every stage of the closing process. It remains unknown whether future regulatory frameworks will allow AI to assume professional liability for errors in settlement details or property appraisals. The requirement to maintain knowledge of fair housing laws resists automation even at this horizon, as these duties involve ethical constraints and social perceptions that are not purely algorithmic.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, brokers function as high-level auditors of automated transaction flows, focusing exclusively on final legal approval and ethical compliance.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the high error cost of real estate transactions maintains a requirement for brokers to manually execute and verify all core settlement and legal tasks.*

"The proven ways real estate agents are using AI to close deals faster." https://www.housingwire.com/articles/brokerages-and-teams-are-rolling-out-ai-assistants-to-reduce-administrative-work-including-lead-intake-crm-updates-offer-drafting-and-call-coaching-with-82-of-agents-using-ai-tools-leaders-incre/
